articles.headline: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Reviews Make It 2026’s Highest Rated Game
keyFacts: Nintendo's remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time achieved a Metascore of 96, making it the highest-rated game of 2026 based on 48 reviews.
Reviewers said the remake remains deeply faithful to the 1998 original while adding quality-of-life improvements like full camera control, motion aiming, and active jumping.
The game is scheduled to be released tomorrow.
body: Nintendo’s much-anticipated remake ofÂ The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is due to reach us tomorrow, and reviews have arrived today. And oh boy, they’re good. Like,Â really good. The Metascore at the time of writing is an epic 96, based on 48 reviews, none of which dips below an 8. And perhaps that’s not a massive surprise given it’s, well, Ocarina of Time, but what a nice relief to learn that Nintendo doesn’t seem to have broken a classic but possibly made it even better. It is, in fact, the highest rated game of 2026. At least for a couple of weeks, anyway.

Review embargoes lifted early this morning, allowing a waterfall of reviews to spill forth, each competing with the next for superlatives to describe the 2026 version of the 1998 original. Appropriately split across two time zones, the remake is deeply faithful to the classic Nintendo 64 version, albeit with a suite of quality-of-life improvements such a running, motion control aiming, and those pesky automatic jumps now being at the behest of a button. There are also embellishments, like how Hyrule Castle Town can now be explored, but reviews are saying nothing has been taken away in the process. (Kotaku did not receive a review copy, and we’ll be reviewing the game once it’s out.)

Eurogamer‘s Christian Donaldson describes both the original and this new version as a “masterpiece,” saying “this is more or less the game that people played back in 1998,” saying even dungeon guides from an old N64 magazine would still get you through here. Keza MacDonald in theÂ Guardian agrees, describing it as “a dream come true” that updates the original game “into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece.”Â Game Informer chimes in on the theme too, Kyle Hilliard calling it “a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element.”

Perhaps one of the most surprising words that keeps being used in reviews is “beautiful.” Early glimpses of the game were met with some horror at the “Nintendo hired that man” impression of an Unreal Engine-looking reimagining of the 30-year-old game. ButÂ Gamespot calls it “gorgeous,”Â Nintendo Life “breathtaking,” andÂ IGN “beautiful.” Really, the only significant criticism I’ve found so far isÂ RPG Site‘s fury that there’s only one save slot (which is, to the site’s credit, idiotic).
Here’s what a selection of reviews are saying:

Despite all of this new sheen, Ocarina of Time retains its understated melancholy. There is an essential tragedy to this tale about a boy hero whose childhood is stolen by an evil king. It is a dark fairytale that begins with a nightmare and the death of a forest god, sometimes scary and, like all childrenâs tales that stand the test of time, totally unpatronising. It is preoccupied with the sadness and inevitability of the passage of time, and the alignment now between that story and the real-world circumstances of this remake is impossible to ignore. The first time I stepped into the Temple of Time and pulled the Master Sword from its stone, I was myself a child. Re-entering that place as an adult gave me shivers I canât quite describe. It got me thinking very deeply about how we pass down our cherished stories to the next generation.

Ocarina of Time is still a wonder of game design and a thrilling adventure. This remake smooths over some rough edges, leaves others intact, and lets what was so special about the original shine through. It can be easy to forget after so many years, but the core structure and design ethos are as strong as they ever were. By approaching this remake with a degree of reverence and respect for the source material, Nintendo has shown that a true masterpiece can stand the test of time.

Was it always this good? Were the dungeons always so complex and challenging, but also so playful, so coherent? Were the bosses always driven by interesting ideas and drama and humour rather than difficulty? Was the world always so rich with minor characters who linger in the mind – the accordion player in the windmill, the gravedigger who has his own tour he’d really like you to try out? It’s impossible for me to say at this point. This is Ocarina as it’s always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday. If you’re new to Zelda and you’re coming to this game fresh, you’re going to love it. Someone, somewhere, is about to play a game so special for the first time that they need to call up their friend and tell them all about it.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it inÂ this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

Whatâs miraculous is how Nintendo is able to retain the grandeur of the world without scaling its locales up beyond recognition. Hyrule is compact by modern game standards, split into only a few tightly designed areas, but it still feels sweeping here. The open air of Hyrule Field is still breathtaking to take in, emphasized with more detailed grass instead of needless space-filling activities. Lake Hylia is just a round body of water, but the glistening light reflecting off of it makes it feel like a cool, serene getaway. Even Kakariko Villageâs graveyard benefits from minor changes, with once low-poly headstones now detailed with embellishments that invite you to pull them to reveal the secrets buried underneath them. The only area that really loses some of its former aura is Hyrule Castle Town, as the pivot to smooth 3D camera controls does away with eerie fixed camera angles that were once so important to selling the villageâs eventual decay.

Hyrule is filled with secrets that exist just to be secrets. Certain ocarina songs trigger interactions that have no purpose other than playfulness. Link can wear masks that change what people say, sometimes revealing shockingly dark secrets. You dive into underground caves to find hidden treasure, but sometimes thereâs just a cow down there! Youâll hear rumors of alternative ways to kill enemies youâll wonder how you ever lived without. There are conversations you can only hear at very specific points that feel really special when you manage to catch them. Ocarina of Time does not care if you miss some of its secrets, which makes stumbling into them all the more impactful. Iâm sure itâs hiding some things that are still a secret to everybody.

Perhaps the Ocarina of Time remakeâs biggest triumph is how it brings a new sense of depth and spectacle to an adventure already rich in cinematic flair. Few games have used the passage of time as emotionally effectively as Ocarina of Time. Returning to familiar places like Lon Lon Ranch or Hyrule Castle as adult Link and discovering what changed in your absence remains a powerful storytelling device, and the remakeâs cinematic presentation makes those moments even more affecting.

The dungeons and puzzles are only the icing for me, though â the story and writing here are the cake. I mentioned the voice acting and visuals already here, but they all combine to add a weight to a story I never previously realized was so moving. Everything is so heightened. From scenes of genuine peril, to quiet moments of haunting loss even amid celebration… I sob. Something about this Ocarina of Time remake moves me like its predecessor didn’t, and I can’t put my finger on whyâ¦ It must be everything about the remake, both its old and new qualities.

articles.headline: Notre Dame faces enormous College Football Playoff test against No. 1 Miami
keyFacts: Eleventh-ranked Notre Dame plays top-ranked Miami in a consequential college football game with major playoff implications.
Committee chair Hunter Yurachek stated that Notre Dame lacks a signature victory to strengthen its postseason résumé.
A win for Notre Dame would improve its ranking, while a loss would drop the team to 7-2 and shrink its playoff margin for error.
body: Notre Dame entered the first College Football Playoff rankings at No. 11, putting the Fighting Irish near the edge of the projected 12-team field. That position makes Saturday's game against No. 1 Miami one of the most consequential contests of the college football season.
Miami is 8-0 and occupies the top spot in the committee's first rankings. Notre Dame is 7-1 and still searching for the kind of signature victory that could strengthen its postseason résumé.
The meeting gives the Fighting Irish an opportunity to address that concern directly. It also creates the possibility of a major shakeup at the top of the rankings.
Miami has earned the committee's respect

The Hurricanes are one of the remaining unbeaten teams in major college football. Their 8-0 record helped them secure the top ranking ahead of Georgia, Utah and Indiana. Miami's placement demonstrates that the committee values its overall performance entering the final month of the regular season.

— Miami Hurricanes Football (@CanesFootball) November 3, 2026
But remaining unbeaten becomes increasingly difficult as opponents recognize the significance of every game.

Notre Dame presents a particularly challenging test because of the program's talent and postseason experience. The Fighting Irish have already lost once, but their current ranking indicates that the committee still considers them a serious contender.
Notre Dame needs a defining victory
Committee chair Hunter Yurachek identified the absence of a signature victory as a concern for Notre Dame. That makes the Miami game especially important.
A win over the nation's top-ranked team would immediately strengthen the Fighting Irish's résumé and likely improve their position in the next rankings.
A loss would create a different situation.

Notre Dame would fall to 7-2 and face increased competition from other teams seeking at-large berths. The Irish would still have opportunities to recover, but their margin for error would become considerably smaller.
MORE: Latest college football news
Saturday could reshape the entire bracket

The Miami-Notre Dame game is only one of several major contests on the schedule. Alabama faces LSU, Kentucky plays Tennessee and Utah meets BYU. Those games involve multiple teams ranked in the initial Top 15. The results could significantly alter the playoff picture before the committee releases its next rankings.
For Notre Dame, however, the stakes are particularly clear. The Fighting Irish have an opportunity to defeat the No. 1 team and answer questions about the strength of their résumé.

Miami has an opportunity to protect its unbeaten record and reinforce its position as the committee's leading national championship contender. That combination makes Saturday's game one of the most important of the season.

articles.headline: Boise State's No. 25 CFP ranking reveals surprising playoff scenario for Ohio State
keyFacts: Boise State entered the initial College Football Playoff rankings at No. 25, which would position the 7-1 Broncos to claim an automatic conference champion berth in the 12-team field.
Automatic qualification rules mean Boise State could reach the playoff while higher-ranked teams like No. 12 Ohio State potentially miss out if the current standings held.
Boise State must continue winning and secure its conference championship to maintain its postseason route, while Ohio State must improve its résumé before the final bracket in December.
body: Boise State entered the first College Football Playoff rankings at No. 25, a position that would normally suggest the Broncos are far from competing for a national championship. But the playoff's automatic qualification rules create a very different possibility.

If the final selections were made using the current rankings, Boise State would occupy the position reserved for the highest-ranked eligible conference champion outside the major conferences. That could allow the Broncos to reach the 12-team field while a higher-ranked team such as Ohio State, currently No. 12, misses out.
The scenario illustrates why the playoff rankings and the projected playoff bracket are not identical.
The 12-team format creates a major distinction
The College Football Playoff uses a 12-team field that includes automatic qualification for the five highest-ranked conference champions, along with seven additional teams selected by the committee.

— CFP (@CFBPlayoff) November 4, 2026
That structure ensures that conference championships matter, even when the committee ranks certain at-large candidates higher.
Boise State is currently the highest-ranked team positioned to benefit from the fifth conference-champion berth. The Broncos are 7-1 and entered the initial rankings at No. 25.

Their path is not guaranteed. Boise State must continue winning and secure the necessary conference championship result. But the current ranking gives the program an identifiable route into the postseason.
Ohio State faces a different challenge

Ohio State is 6-2 and ranked No. 12. That position would normally place the Buckeyes on the edge of the playoff field, but automatic qualification can reduce the number of available at-large positions.

The Buckeyes must improve their résumé enough to avoid relying on the final available spot. Other teams ranked near the cutoff face similar uncertainty, including Notre Dame at No. 11 and several two-loss contenders.
Every remaining game can influence the final order.
MORE: College football schedule, scores
The bracket will change before December
The first rankings are only an early snapshot. Conference championship results, head-to-head games and potential upsets will reshape the field.
Boise State could climb, fall or lose its projected automatic qualification position entirely. But the current scenario provides an important reminder for fans evaluating the playoff picture.
Being ranked higher than another team does not necessarily guarantee receiving a postseason invitation ahead of that opponent.

The selection format rewards certain conference champions, and Boise State currently stands to benefit. For Ohio State and other teams near the cutoff, that makes every remaining result especially important.

articles.headline: Richard Young keeps Colorado football’s starting running back job
keyFacts: Deion Sanders confirmed that Richard Young will start his second straight game at running back for Colorado against Arizona State.
Young earned the starting role after rushing for 120 yards and two touchdowns in an overtime win against Kansas State.
Colorado enters the upcoming game with a 3-5 record seeking to build upon the momentum from ending a five-game losing streak.
body: Richard Young will get another opportunity to lead Colorado 's backfield Saturday at Arizona State after making the most of his first start for the Buffaloes.

Deion Sanders confirmed Tuesday that Young will start his second straight game after a 120-yard, two-touchdown performance in Colorado's 27-24 overtime win over Kansas State . The Alabama transfer carried 24 times after receiving no more than eight rushing attempts in any previous game this season.
"The more carries that I was getting, the more hungry I was getting," Young said Tuesday.
Young's patience leads to a larger role

Young's opportunity expanded following an injury to Micah Welch. His performance made him Colorado's second 100-yard rusher during Sanders' four seasons, joining Welch, who reached the mark against Weber State earlier this year.
Sanders credited Young for continuing to work through limited playing time and said the fourth-year running back never had a "pity party."
"He hadn't got his opportunity, a true opportunity, and he got it," Sanders said. "And that's the most touches he’s ever had in a college football game. So he proved that he's more than worthy."

Back on the @CUBuffsFootball beat today as #CoachPrime @DeionSanders held his weekly press conference along with Buffs’ DE Yamil Talib, RB Richard Young and DB Ben Finneseth. CU hits the road for a @Big12Conference clash against Arizona State on Saturday. #GoBuffs #SkoBuffs pic.twitter.com/VmTBVfsRP2

— Michael Lyle, Jr. 🎧🎙 (@LyleMultimedia) November 3, 2026 Young arrived with a recruiting resume that included ESPN's No. 22 national ranking in the 2023 class. Nick Saban signed him at Alabama , where Young received 23 carries during the entire 2025 season.
Asked whether something changed in practice last week, Sanders said he had seen Young's ability "from the beginning."
"Sooner or later you gotta say, 'He's in,’" Sanders said.
Colorado gets help for Isaac Wilson
Young's production helped quarterback Isaac Wilson complete his first interception-free start after throwing seven interceptions across his previous three starts.

Colorado enters Saturday at 3-5 , with Young's second start offering an opportunity to build on a rushing performance that helped end a five-game losing streak. His workload against Arizona State will show how prominently the Buffaloes plan to feature him throughout November.

articles.headline: 20 Years Later, Bong Joon-Ho Looks Back at His Sci-Fi Thriller Masterpiece: 'It Was a Very Tough Process'
keyFacts: Director Bong Joon-ho's 2006 sci-fi thriller film The Host is celebrating its 20th anniversary with a 4K remaster returning to theaters on November 20, 2026.
Bong said the film's monster was inspired by high school stress, his view of the Han River, and his fascination with the Loch Ness monster.
Bong stated that the 4K remaster features no digital changes to the film, and the team's goal was simply to recreate the feel of a 35-millimeter print.
body: Two decades ago, in a 2006 interview with a Korean newspaper, Bong Joon-ho made a surprising statement about his then-new horror movie, The Host. The director, who would go on to make Parasite, Snowpiercer, and Mickey 17, revealed that the mutated monster from The Host was based on an actual creature he'd spotted in Seoul’s Han River, 19 years earlier.
"I don't know exactly what it was," Bong said at the time. "What is clear is that it was a living creature, and it wasn't human. Its size was probably similar to a monster from a movie."

I came across this bizarre detail while doing research on The Host for an interview with Bong himself. (The film turns 20 this year and is celebrating with a 4K remaster and a return to theaters.) So when I get on a Zoom call with the director, it's one of the first things I ask about.
"Attending high school comes with a lot of pressure," Bong tells Polygon. "So that's maybe what led to that kind of a delusion."

OK, mystery solved. Bong Joon-ho didn't actually see a mutated river monster when he was in high school, but he did imagine one under the pressure of college-placement exams. (His youthful obsession with another famous monster might have contributed, too, but we'll get to that in a minute.)

Read on as Bong answers six of our most pressing questions about The Host, while also teasing his upcoming animated feature, Ally, which shares a surprising connection with the 20-year-old monster movie.
1 What's different about this new 4K version of The Host?

Ahead of the interview, I received a digital copy of the remaster and watched a few of my favorite scenes. This new version of The Host looks amazing, especially the CGI used to create the film's iconic monster. I wondered if perhaps Bong and his team had done some touch-ups on the creature, especially since the original film had a famously small budget. But according to the director, no specific changes were made to the film.

"Our overall goal in the restoration was to recreate that feeling of watching a 35-millimeter print, the highest quality print on the first day of release," Bong says. "Of course, it was a digital restoration, but that was our goal to use the digital restoration to create that film look of watching the film on a high quality print for the first time. There wasn't anything that we changed digitally."
2 So did Bong Joon-ho actually see a river monster in high school?
Again, the answer is no, but Bong's full response reveals even more about the early inspirations for what would eventually become The Host.

"Attending a Korean high school comes with a lot of pressure," he says. “It's a very tough environment. So I must have been in a pretty fragile mental state back then, where I was having some sort of delusion."
That said, Bong points to two other factors that might explain why he thought he saw a monster back then — and how we wound up with a movie like The Host in the first place.

"What was not a delusion were two facts," he says. "The first fact is that the place that I was living in at the time, our apartment was near the Han River, and I would see the river every day. And the second fact is that I was very fond of the Loch Ness monster. I would try to seek out articles and photographs of the Loch Ness monster. And so those two things combined in my mind, the fact that I was seeing the Han River every day and I imagined what if a monster like the Loch Ness monster appeared in this river that is right in front of me."
3 Will he ever return to horror?

While plenty of Bong's movies have horror elements (Parasite has some moments of terrifying tension), he's never truly returned to the genre since making The Host. According to the director, that may change soon.

"It's not a monster movie, but there are horror thriller ideas that I'm developing at the moment," he says. "My iPad is always filled with movie ideas, and there are five right now that are becoming more specific. And out of the five, two of them could be classified as horror."
He also notes that while his next movie, Ally, definitely is not a horror film, the upcoming animated feature does have one thing in common with The Host.

"I'm in the middle of the post-production of my new animation movie," Bong says. "It has many creatures, and one of the creatures really looks like a monster, but a very funny monster. He's quite the character."
4 How the American military (and American movies) inspired The Host

The inciting incident in The Host involves an American doctor ordering his Korean subordinate to pour a large amount of formaldehyde into a drain that dumps into the Han River, which leads to the creation of the mutated monster. This scene draws on a real incident that directly inspired Bong's movie.

"The scene of the formaldehyde being dumped is based on an actual event, the McFarland Incident, that happened in 2000 in Korea," he says. "At the time, there were a lot of environmental groups that were protesting in Korea. That actually felt like the beginning of a horror film to me."
The other direct inspiration for The Host's premise is pure fiction.

"Maybe you remember a movie called Alligator — a very interesting American monster movie from the 1980s," Bong says. "That movie has a similar beginning. There's a chemical experiment and they release a baby alligator into the sewers. That alligator later becomes this huge monster. That's a film that I was really fond of at the time."
"Those two ideas combined and that led to the political satire and everything else that's shown in The Host."
5 Was Godzilla an influence?

In previous interviews, Bong has pointed to his love for the Godzilla movies as a direct inspiration for The Host, but when I bring this up now, he deflects, pointing instead to two other fan-favorite monster movies.

"I liked the Godzilla films when I was younger. I would see them on TV. And I was also fascinated by the characters that appeared with Godzilla, like Mothra. But Godzilla didn't directly influence The Host," Bong says. "The monsters are very different in size. I wanted a monster that wasn't destroying buildings, but was more realistic and could be found in real life — a monster that could possibly hide between buses."
"At the time of making The Host, I was probably more influenced by Ridley Scott's Alien and John Carpenter's The Thing. So I was actually drawn to monsters that are smaller in size."
6 How Bong filmed The Host's epic final scene

The Host centers on the Park family, led by the lazy and buffoonish Gang-du (Song Kang-ho), who are struggling to get by even before the monster steals Gang-du's daughter and disappears. At the climax, the Parks reunite and face off against the beast in a thrilling sequence that ends in a hard-earned victory and an emotional family reunion.
The ending more than holds up 20 years later, especially with this stunning remaster, but looking back now, the primary emotion Bong recalls from shooting that scene is embarrassment.

"The problem was, it was at a real location, the riverbank," Bong says. “It was not a soundstage, like the Alien movies. A lot of people were there watching the very famous Korean stars doing something on the riverbank. But unfortunately, there was no monster on set, of course. So we were doing very strange things in the air. We were pretending that there was something there. Song Kang-ho was already a huge superstar in Korea at the time, and he was screaming and doing these crazy things and people were watching and wondering like, 'What the hell is he doing?'"
Shooting that moment, we just felt embarrassed.

"Shooting that moment, we just felt embarrassed. We were just hoping they would watch the film later with actual VFX. But that's the predominant emotion I remember from shooting that scene: embarrassment."
When storyboarding the scene, Bong also had to be extremely sparing in his use of the monster due to the film's limited budget.

"It was a very tough process because we had a super limited budget for VFX," he says. "If you actually rewatch it again and count the number of times the monster is actually shown in its entirety, it's actually not many shots. I could only use seven shots of the monster in this sequence."

"Without the monster in the frame, I had to make the audience feel the existence and the scariness of the monster. I had to maintain the terror throughout the scene. I had to think about how am I gonna do that without actually showing the creature? And in the end, I believe that led me to be more creative."
The Host returns to theaters on Nov. 20, 2026. Tickets are available now.

articles.headline: Eleventh-hour election interventions
keyFacts: Representative Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul el Sayed in Michigan following intraparty policy fractures.
Late political interventions target uncommitted voters across eleven competitive Senate seats where minor shifts can alter legislative control.
Election results will determine whether the eleventh-hour intervention successfully impacted late-deciding voters as polls close.
body: Medical interventions require precise timing. A treatment administered too early might lack sufficient diagnostic data. A treatment administered too late will fail to alter the outcome.

The late-stage foreign policy announcement represented an unprecedented eleventh-hour political intervention. In a hyper-polarized landscape, where the battle for control of Congress rests on razor-thin margins, we must analyze whether a sudden executive policy shift can truly sway late-deciding voters.

The focus centers on 11 highly competitive Senate seats, including six consensus toss-ups, as well as critical swing districts in states like Michigan . Traditional campaign strategies rely on months of steady narrative building. In contrast, an Election Day policy shock targets the specific subset of voters who remain genuinely uncommitted as they approach the ballot box. It seeks to disrupt existing calculations, break partisan gridlock, and suppress or elevate specific turnout metrics in localized precincts.

This disruption manifested directly on the ground in the final 48 hours of the election cycle. In Michigan, the race exploded when progressive Democratic nominee Abdul el Sayed faced a stunning eleventh-hour defection from his former primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI), who crossed party lines to endorse Republican nominee Mike Rogers. The sudden shift was explicitly triggered by intraparty fractures over Middle Eastern foreign policy and domestic spending priorities. It forced both campaigns into a frantic, last-minute sprint to mobilize competing factions of the electorate on Election Day.
THE PROBLEM ISN’T THAT THE POPE VOTED

Historical data suggests that late-breaking developments rarely cause a total realignment of the electorate. Most voters have already solidified their choices weeks in advance through early voting mechanisms. Yet, in states where historic margins are decided by a few thousand votes, a minor shift among late deciders can entirely alter the legislative balance of power. The morning announcement serves as a final, high-stakes attempt to dictate the closing media cycle and force a late-stage recalculation.

The tactical approach reflects a broader trend in modern political behavior. When structural institutions fail to deliver predictable outcomes, leaders resort to disruptive, high-visibility actions to force immediate results. The long-term consequences on international relationships are deferred. The immediate priority is the acquisition of institutional control. As the polls close, the metric of success for this intervention will be written entirely in the results.

Eric Wargotz is a practicing physician, geopolitical analyst, and multisector policy writer whose commentary has appeared in the Washington Examiner , the Baltimore Sun , and the Jerusalem Post . He is a judge and the 178th president of MedChi, the Maryland State Medical Society, following a career that includes serving as a Senate nominee and elected county commission president. A clinical professor emeritus at George Washington University, his views are his own and do not represent his affiliates.

articles.headline: A Turkish UN secretary-general would serve the Erdogan regime
keyFacts: Turkey nominated Feridun Sinirlioglu as a candidate for the top United Nations secretary-general position on Friday.
The author argues that Sinirlioglu's career representing the Turkish government's policies makes him unfit for the independent role.
Critics cite Sinirlioglu's past actions regarding Cyprus, Russia, maritime boundaries, and human rights as violations of international norms.
body: Turkey has nominated a serious candidate for the top United Nations post, one which Feridun Sinirlioglu must not be allowed to hold. Selecting a Turkish U.N. secretary-general would transform the U.N. into a puppet show for Turkey’s authoritarian regime led by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Given Ankara’s flagrant violations of international law, appointing Sinirlioglu would be an insult to the rules-based international order.

The U.N. was founded in 1945 and consists of 193 member states. Its mission is to maintain international peace and security, provide humanitarian assistance to those in need, protect human rights, and uphold international law. As the U.N.’s chief administrative officer, the secretary-general represents the organization’s values and serves as a voice for all humanity, particularly the world’s poorest and most vulnerable populations. The position therefore demands unwavering independence, impartiality, and a commitment to upholding the principles of the U.N. Charter.
This is not the job for a Turkish candidate, who has represented and defended Ankara’s indefensible views on the world stage for decades.

On Friday, Turkey nominated Sinirlioglu, the eighth secretary general of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, appointed in December 2024. He briefly served as Turkey’s Minister of Foreign Affairs in 2015. Before that, he built a long and distinguished career as a diplomat in Turkey’s foreign ministry.

In short, he has played a significant role in representing Ankara’s policies and priorities, raising questions about his ability to maintain the independence expected of a U.N. secretary-general. While Turkey has faced multiple criticisms over its domestic and foreign policy , Sinirlioglu has never publicly distanced himself from Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party policies and has instead represented the government in several important diplomatic roles.

One key policy area is Cyprus. Turkey invaded the island in 1974 and, in 1984, declared the territory it occupies as the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, an entity which only Turkey recognizes. As an employee of the Turkish foreign ministry, Sinirlioglu has helped uphold one of the biggest violations of national sovereignty, something the U.N. Security Council has denounced numerous times. As U.N. chief, there is sufficient alarmism to suspect that Sinirlioglu would push a policy agenda over Cyprus: the formal recognition of the TRNC, which would be a big win for Erdogan, and a major loss for international law.

Another issue is Sinirlioglu’s support of other states that violate international law. As OSCE chief, he has called Russia an “important partner” and thanked Moscow’s foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, for engaging in a “frank and productive” conversation about the Russia-Ukraine conflict . Defenders of the rules-based order should not be enabling states which violate national borders and terrorize innocent people, a principle which Sinirlioglu has chosen to ignore.

As Turkey’s U.N. ambassador, Sinirlioglu also played a pivotal role in Ankara’s effort to redraw the boundaries of the Eastern Mediterranean, illegally and unilaterally. In letters to the U.N. secretary-general between July 2021 and 2022, he argued that Greece’s sovereignty over these islands depended on keeping them demilitarized under the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne and the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty. Greece rejected the claim as legally baseless, warning it threatened regional peace and stability. To be clear, Turkey has refused to sign the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea and instead is seeking to expand its maritime borders at the expense of Greece, Cyprus, and possibly other countries along the Mediterranean littoral under its “Blue Homeland” doctrine. As the U.N. chief, how can Sinirlioglu be expected to uphold established maritime law when he has devoted his career to undermining it?
THE ICC EARNED ITS RECKONING. STILL, RUBIO SHOULD NOT WRECK IT

Finally, Sinirlioglu’s close association with the Turkish government’s policies also raises questions about the value he ascribes to human rights. In 2021, Turkey withdrew from the Istanbul Convention, an international agreement aimed at preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence signed by 45 European countries. The Turkish government terminated the convention despite widespread societal and international criticism. By any measure, Erdogan’s governance of Turkey since 2003 has been characterized by devastating blows to the rule of law, freedom of expression, and citizens’ rights , something on which, once again, Sinirlioglu has had nothing to say.

As a senior diplomat, Sinirlioglu certainly has a resume that makes him qualified to hold the top U.N. job, but that is necessary but not sufficient. He has also represented a country which consistently and proudly violates established international norms, laws, and practices. A representative of the Erdogan regime has no business running the U.N.
Sinan Ciddi is a senior fellow and director of the Turkey program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies in Washington, where Helin Unal is a research fellow.

articles.headline: Google hasn’t figured out how to make AI pay like its search engine
keyFacts: Alphabet reported that Google's Search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent year over year in the third quarter while paid clicks growth dropped to 8 percent.
Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said currency effects and Google's AI makeover contributed to the slowdown because AI queries monetize at a lower rate.
Google is currently expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode as the company and its competitors continue figuring out how to monetize AI search.
body: Search queries are growing at their fastest rate in five years, Google parent Alphabet said in its earnings report last week. However, Google’s Search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent year over year in the third quarter, down from roughly 17 percent in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, growth in paid clicks — clicks on ads that generate revenue for Google — slowed from 13 percent to 8 percent.
Google hasn’t figured out how to make AI pay like its search engine
Google says AI is boosting searches, but that activity isn’t translating into faster growth for the business that pays for it.

That’s still substantial growth, but not the direction investors were hoping for from a company planning to spend about $200 billion this year on infrastructure, largely to support AI. Alphabet shares have fallen about 14 percent since it reported earnings last week, as investors question the costs and returns of the company’s AI ambitions.
“This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades.”

Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said currency effects were the biggest driver of the revenue-growth slowdown, alongside changes in spending by advertisers in particular industries. But Google’s AI makeover also contributed to the slowdown: AI Mode queries were growing strongly but monetizing at a lower rate than traditional searches, Schindler says. He added that Google feels good about its trajectory and that its “ad experiments have shown promising results.”
It remains unclear whether that reflects a deliberate rollout of ads, as Google says, or a more fundamental problem with advertising in AI search.
YOY growth for search revenue vs. paid clicks in Q1-3 in 2026

“This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades,” Nate Elliott, an eMarketer principal analyst covering AI and advertising, tells The Verge. AI is changing how people find information — and whether they click on the ads that fund Google’s business.

What Google’s core Search business looks like increasingly depends on what you ask. In many cases, AI Overviews add generated summaries to search results; electing AI Mode turns searching into a conversation. But someone searching for Nikes can still get familiar shopping listings and text ads, says Andy Taylor, vice president of research at digital advertising agency Tinuiti. They’re looking to buy shoes rather than get an AI explanation of them.

Google’s argument is that AI is expanding the business. Schindler says most AI Mode queries are “incremental” — additional questions rather than replacements for existing searches. Many are also “upper-funnel,” meaning people are researching potential purchases before they know what they want. The company sees those searches as opportunities to sell more ads over time.

Google is currently expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode, including internationally and across multiple turns of US AI Mode conversations. It has also floated bringing ads to its standalone Gemini app, saying formats developed for AI Mode could carry over, but hasn’t announced when.

The thing is, Google, as well as competitors like OpenAI, are still figuring out how to make ads work in AI — both delivering results for advertisers and avoiding alienating the people using their AI tools.

For now, advertisers are still getting results from Google. Tinuiti’s same-store advertisers increased their Google paid search spending 14 percent year over year in the third quarter while maintaining their return-on-ad-spend targets.
“If people are clicking through less often. That is a challenge that they need to figure out.”
“We’re still seeing a good return, and we’re not seeing performance take a hit,” Taylor says.

The catch is that advertisers can’t isolate how Google’s AI ads are doing. Google doesn’t let them separately target that inventory or break out its performance, Taylor says. Steady overall returns could mean AI ad traffic is still too small to noticeably affect the results, or that it performs similarly to existing inventory. Taylor suspects it’s mostly the former.

That leaves an important question unanswered: How much will AI add to Google’s advertising business, and how much could it replace? Additional queries could bring in new revenue even if each earns less than a traditional search. The risk is that AI Mode also draws people away from searches that Google monetizes more effectively. Google’s claim that most AI Mode queries are additional doesn’t tell us how much revenue it could lose from the searches AI Mode replaces.
“If people are clicking through less often,” Elliott says, “that is a challenge that they need to figure out.”

The promise of conversational advertising is that people share much more about their needs than they would in a few keywords. But platforms still have to identify which parts of a conversation matter and match them with the right ads.
“It’s not a slam dunk that it’s going to turn into more effective advertising,” Elliott says.

An early study of ChatGPT ads suggests richer conversations don’t automatically translate into more retail sales. An October working paper found that US visits from ChatGPT ads generated 64 percent less revenue for retailers per session than visits from Google Search ads: $0.89 versus $2.45. The working paper measures retailers’ sales rather than platform revenue, and its findings about ChatGPT don’t establish how Google’s own AI ads perform.

Taylor cautions that those comparisons depend on what people are searching for. Someone searching Google for Nike shoes may already be ready to buy, while someone asking an AI tool which running shoes to choose is still researching. A higher sales return could reflect that difference in purchase intent rather than more effective ads.

Google’s existing business has given it room to take its time with AI ads, Taylor says. He points to its successful shift to mobile: Early phone traffic was less valuable to advertisers because shopping on a phone was cumbersome, but that changed.

Elliott cautions that finding effective ad formats can take years. Search engines started with banner ads before adopting paid listings; social media went through its own experimentation. Today’s formats may not be the ones that ultimately work.
But Google’s mounting AI spending raises the stakes. Search revenue is still growing by double digits, but the company has yet to show how well its new way of searching can pay.
“They absolutely do not have it all figured out,” Elliott says. “No one has it all figured out.”

articles.headline: West Ham held talks with ex-Premier League star before Scott Parker decision
keyFacts: West Ham reportedly held talks with John Heitinga about becoming manager before appointing Scott Parker on a two-and-a-half-year contract.
Parker replaced Nuno Espirito Santo, who was sacked by West Ham following successive home defeats to Southampton and West Brom.
Parker will meet his new players on Wednesday ahead of an away league match against Cardiff.
body: West Ham reportedly held talks with John Heitinga over succeeding Nuno Espirito Santo before the club settled on Scott Parker.
The Hammers named their former captain as their new manager on a two-and-a-half-year contract 24 hours after firing Nuno .
Nuno was sacked by West Ham after 14 months in charge Getty
The East Londoners pulled the trigger on the former Wolves gaffer following successive home defeats to Southampton and West Brom .
However, despite the rapid turnaround within the dugout, the Irons still considered other potential successors to the 52-year-old.
John Heitinga held talks with West Ham
According to The Athletic, West Ham held talks with Heitinga about potentially replacing Nuno before and after the loss to West Brom.
The report adds that the Dutchman was interested in the role, but Mark Noble instead encouraged Daniel Kretinsky to appoint Parker.
Heitinga was previously West Ham’s assistant coach between September 2023 and May 2024, during David Moyes’ tenure in charge.
The 42-year-old has been out of work since leaving his role as Tottenham’s number two in February.
Heitinga’s Spurs exit came amid Thomas Frank’s firing , which happened just 33 days after he joined the Dane’s backroom staff .
The former Everton and Fulham player’s last job as a head coach came prior to his arrival in north London.
Heitinga, who departed his position as Arne Slot’s assistant at Liverpool in the summer of 2025 following the Reds’ Premier League title triumph , took up the post at Ajax .
Heitinga held assistant coaching roles at Liverpool and Tottenham Getty
Heitinga’s record as a manager
The 87-cap Netherlands international only won five matches in his five months as the main man in the dugout of the Dutch giants.

Towards the end of his reign, Ronald de Boer labelled Ajax as a club in ‘crisis’ on talkSPORT, while European football expert Andy Brassell admitted Heitinga’s appointment was a ‘real backward step’ .
Ironically, it was a defeat to West Brom that saw West Ham register their interest in his services, with Heitinga previously attracting managerial interest from the Baggies themselves in 2025 .
Parker, meanwhile, will meet his new players on Wednesday ahead of their away league match with Cardiff, which is live on talkSPORT2.
The Englishman, who has achieved Championship promotion three times in his managerial career with Fulham , Bournemouth and Burnley , was available as a free agent after leaving the Clarets in April.
Parker has been appointed West Ham manager Getty

Parker said: “It is a very proud moment for me to step into this role and return to a club that means so much to me and my family. A lot of very fond memories of my time here – four years of probably the best football I played in my career.

“There was a warmth, a love, a feeling that I probably didn’t have anywhere else. There was something which stood out constantly and that was the relationship that I built up with the fanbase here. That rapport and respect, that I felt instantly.

“More than anything, this is an opportunity that I am very excited about. I feel privileged and honoured to be the guy that wants to lead us back to the Premier League and be the head coach of this football club at this moment in time.

“My energy levels, my enthusiasm, my desire, my passion – it’s absolutely running through and that’s the feeling I had as soon as there was a conversation that this was possible. That’s exactly why I’m here and why I want to be here.

“From my first calls with Karim [Virani] and Daniel [Křetínský], it was clear they have a shared vision and desire to return the club to the Premier League as quickly as possible. I share that ambition and I’m very confident we can achieve it.

“I’ve been in this division three times and I’ve got out of this division three times. This is a tough division, there is absolutely no denying it. And I will use every ounce of my experience, every ounce of my knowledge, to have an understanding of what we’re going to need to bring consistency.

“And that’s going to be the key word for all of us really. The consistency of what we do and the commitment levels that we go to will give us the best opportunity to get out of this division and be the team that we can be.”

articles.headline: Canva lays off over 1,200 people amid slowing growth
keyFacts: Design software maker Canva is laying off 22% of its staff, or 1,271 people, due to slowing growth and ballooning AI costs.
CEO Melanie Perkins stated in a note to employees that the company must change its structure and reduce subspecialisation to address these challenges.
The company is also reshuffling its organizational chart, merging teams, shifting to hybrid work, and reducing its revenue growth forecast to 20%.
body: Design software maker Canva is cutting 22% of its staff, amounting to 1,271 people, amid a growth slowdown.
The company’s co-founder and CEO, Melanie Perkins, in a note to employees said while Canva has scaled so far, it needs to change to address slowing growth.

“Over the past thirteen years, we’ve turned a dream in a pitch deck into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people. None of it would have been possible without the talent, imagination, and care of every single person who has been part of this journey. Yet success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next. This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade,” Perkins wrote.

Canva is reshuffling its organizational chart and merging its product, growth and platform teams to reduce communication friction. The company is also reducing “subspecialisation,” which means its employees might be asked to take up more responsibilities. The company is also moving towards hybrid work and asking people to work from an office a few days a week.

The company has been shipping its own AI models to reduce costs and reliance on third-party models, but it still had to cut its revenue growth forecast to 20% from 30% to address ballooning AI costs. This also resulted in Canva’s early investors cutting its valuation to about $35 billion earlier this year.

Canva is also facing increasing competition from AI startups and general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, whose image generation capabilities allow people to easily put together posters and presentations.

Captain X is a battle pass-only outfit that cannot be unlocked early and will become available on November 21.
There are seven total rewards in the Captain X series that unlock progressively as players finish varying numbers of weekly tasks.
body: There are many unique skins you can unlock in Fortnite Treasure Hunters. One of the toughest ones to get your hands on is Captain X, a battle pass Outfit that requires quite a bit of progression to obtain.

This style will only be around and available to earn through quests in this season, so if you’re interested in adding it to your collection, you’ve got to get to work on it fast. Since Treasure Hunters is a mini-season, you’ve got quite a limited amount of time to work on it, so here’s how to get Captain X and all of his rewards in Fortnite .

articles.headline: West Ham confirm Parker as boss
keyFacts: West Ham United appointed former midfielder Scott Parker as their new head coach on a two-and-a-half-year contract following the sacking of Nuno Espirito Santo.
Parker will take charge of the team for the first time when West Ham play Cardiff City in the Championship on Wednesday.
Interim chief executive Karim Virani stated that the board unanimously chose Parker because of his proven promotion record in the EFL Championship and his deep understanding of the club.
body: - Published
West Ham United have confirmed the appointment of former midfielder Scott Parker as their new head coach on a two-and-a-half-year contract.
The 46-year-old replaces Nuno Espirito Santo, who was sacked on Tuesday after the club's disappointing start to the Championship season.
Parker previously led Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley to promotion from the Championship, but has been out of work since leaving the Clarets in April after their relegation from the Premier League.
He will take charge of the team for the first time on Wednesday when West Ham travel to Cardiff City in the Championship.
First-team coaches Steve Potts, Gerard Prenderville and Billy Lepine will assist Parker while his former team-mate Mark Noble will also work closely with him in his role as sporting director.
The club will also make further announcements on the backroom team in the coming days and weeks.
"It is a very proud moment for me to step into this role and return to a club that means so much to me and my family," Parker told the club website., external

"There was a warmth, a love, a feeling that I probably didn't have anywhere else. There was something which stood out constantly and that was the relationship that I built up with the fanbase here. That rapport and respect, that I felt instantly.

"More than anything, this is an opportunity that I am very excited about. I feel privileged and honoured to be the guy that wants to lead us back to the Premier League and be the head coach of this football club at this moment in time.

"My energy levels, my enthusiasm, my desire, my passion - it's absolutely running through and that's the feeling I had as soon as there was a conversation that this was possible. That's exactly why I'm here and why I want to be here."
'I've got out of this division three times'
Parker quickly became the front-runner for the job after the sacking of Nuno, which followed back-to-back home defeats by Southampton and West Bromwich Albion.

He becomes West Ham's fourth permanent manager since David Moyes left London Stadium in May 2024, and joins with the pre-season promotion favourites sitting eighth in the Championship table, six points behind leaders Middlesbrough.

"From my first calls with Karim [Virani, interim chief executive] and Daniel [Kretinsky, largest shareholder], it was clear they have a shared vision and desire to return the club to the Premier League as quickly as possible. I share that ambition and I'm very confident we can achieve it," he added.
"I've been in this division three times and I've got out of this division three times. This is a tough division, there is absolutely no denying it.
"I will use every ounce of my experience, every ounce of my knowledge, to have an understanding of what we're going to need to bring consistency."
He joins a club that has had a stuttering start to life in the Championship after relegation last season.

They have won two of their past six games and have lost back-to-back home matches - going down 3-2 to Southampton and then 3-1 to West Brom on Saturday - losses that have seen them drop down from second place.

The departures of players including Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville, El Hadji Malick Diouf, James Ward-Prowse and Freddie Potts secured the club about Â£150m in transfer revenue over the summer following their relegation.
They used some of that cash to pay Celtic a Championship record Â£22m for midfielder Arne Engels and spent a reported Â£12m on Norwegian winger Edvin Austbo.

Experienced campaigners Joel Veltman and Manor Solomon also joined on free transfers from Brighton and Tottenham respectively while they kept key players such as England winger Jarrod Bowen, Czech midfielder Tomas Soucek and Greek defender Konstantinos Mavropanos.
It is a squad that Parker needs to galvanise if the 2023 Uefa Europa Conference League winners are to return to the top flight at the first time of asking.
"He is someone who is held in high regard at West Ham United and throughout the game, and he was the unanimous choice of the board to become our new head coach," Virani said.

"He has fantastic experience and pedigree across an outstanding playing and coaching career, a clear and proven track record of success as a head coach in the EFL Championship, and a deep understanding of West Ham United, its identity and our loyal and passionate fanbase.
"We believe that all of these factors together make him the right man to lead us forward and help the club to achieve our objectives this season and beyond.

"Scott has the complete support of everyone here and, from the conversations we have had with him already, we believe he will represent West Ham United and our supporters in a way that we can all be extremely proud of."
Can Parker get West Ham back to the Premier League and keep them there?
Parker's managerial career to date has seen three promotions followed by much leaner times in the Premier League.
His first taste of senior management was at Fulham, who he immediately guided back to the Premier League with a play-off final win over Brentford in 2020.

Parker could not keep them up again the following season and left by mutual consent in June 2021. He then became manager of Bournemouth and led them to promotion as runners-up, ironically behind Fulham.
A few weeks into the new Premier League season, the Cherries lost 9-0 at Liverpool and Parker departed three days later.
He briefly managed Belgian side Club Brugge in the 2022-23 season before replacing the Bayern Munich-bound Vincent Kompany as Burnley boss in 2024.
Parker guided the Clarets to the Premier League at the first attempt, with one of the best defensive records in English football history and a 31-match unbeaten streak.
However, he could not keep the team up last season and he departed Turf Moor after their relegation was confirmed.
Parker is highly regarded at West Ham from his four years as a player at the club.
Having emerged at Charlton Athletic, and endured an unsuccessful move to Chelsea in 2004, he joined the Hammers from Newcastle United in June 2007, for a fee of Â£7m.
Parker went on to make 129 appearances in claret and blue, scoring 12 goals. He also won the club's player of the year award three seasons in a row.

In 2010-11, despite the Hammers' relegation from the Premier League, Parker also won the Football Writers' Association footballer of the year award and was nominated for the Professional Footballers' Association player of the year.
He started the first four Championship matches of West Ham's 2011â12 campaign, but handed in a transfer request after a bid came in from Tottenham Hotspur.
Parker completed a move to Spurs in order to further his England career, and he went on to be part of Roy Hodgson's Euro 2012 squad.
He later played for Fulham, before retiring in June 2017.
Why was this move not made in the summer? - analysis

As soon as the news broke that Nuno Espirito Santo had been relieved of his duties at West Ham it became clear that the club had identified Scott Parker as the coach they believed could lead them back to the Premier league at the first time of asking.
The only nagging question for me was why this move was not made in the summer giving Parker time to build a squad he would want and have pre-season to prepare them.

Parker's pedigree of guiding clubs to promotion from the second tier in his first full year in charge is unquestionable having done it at Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley. These achievements were at clubs where there was an expectation of success so the fact that West Ham have the same aim this season will not faze him.
He follows in the footsteps of the great Billy Bonds, the only other former captain to go on and manage West Ham. Bonds was also charged with gaining promotion, something he achieved.
There is no doubt where the issues have been for West Ham so far this season, starting games slowly, conceding first and on a number of occasions conceding too many.

Parker will bring structure and clarity to the team, providing a stable platform from which the front line can start exploiting their talents. He will want to quickly create an identity and will leave players in no doubt that hard work and commitment lead to positive outcomes.

The question of 'style' had been on the lips of a number of people in regards to Parker and much was made of Burnley's incredible parsimony during their promotion to the Premier League under him, but they were also the third highest scorers and gained 100 points, which is no mean feat.
He has players at his disposal to be effective going forward, and the coaching ability to make a rather leaky side more watertight.
The fans and the club will hope that is the perfect formula.

articles.headline: Five takeaways from Democrats’ historic midterm blue tsunami
keyFacts: Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress and a majority of state governorships in the midterm elections.
Democrats won major races in Texas, Kansas, Maine, and Ohio amid widespread voter dissatisfaction with President Trump.
Incoming Democratic committee leaders announced plans to issue subpoenas and launch investigations into President Trump's administration.
body: The worst-case scenario for Republicans unfolded in Tuesday’s midterm elections, as Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress as well as a majority of state governorships.
Here are 5 takeaways from the historic GOP shellacking:
Trump’s ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ plea fails miserably
The president repeatedly urgedhis supporters to pretend he was up for election during his cross-country blitz in the weeks leading up to Tuesday.
Voters clearly heard him, just not in the way Trump intended.
Exit poll results released by the Associated Press showed 71% of voters said Congress must do more to check the commander-in-chief, while 62% directly blamed the president for higher prices.
Three-quarters of voters indicated they were “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the direction of the country and more than six in ten disapproved of Trump’s performance.

As a result, control of both the House and Senate changed hands in the same midterm for the first time since 2006 — also during the second term of a Republican president waging a controversial war in the Middle East.

Democrats won without regard for geography or political history. In Maine, Troy Jackson defeated 30-year incumbent Susan Collins. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became just the second Democrat ever elected to the Senate from the Sunflower State — and first since George McGill in 1932.
In Ohio, Amy Acton became just the second Democrat since 1990 to be elected governor.
And then, of course, there’s Texas.
Texas chooses blue

The Lone Star State was emblematic of how the night went for Republicans, with Democrat James Talarico defeating Republican Ken Paxton by a whopping 12 percentage points for the party’s first Senate race victory since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.
Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, seeking a fourth term in office, was also swamped by the blue wave, losing to Democratic state lawmaker Gina Hinojosa by seven points.

The GOP fared little better in House races, with Rep. Monica De La Cruz defeated by Democrat Bobby Pulido in the 15th Congressional District, while the 23rd Congressional District, whose seat had been left vacant since ex-Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) resigned in April, was won by Democrat Katy Padilla Stout.
Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez – two of the top targets of a GOP-friendly mid-decade redistricting – easily bested their GOP rivals as well.
Democrats promise deluge
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, had a simple message for the White House as results rolled in on election night.
“LAWYER UP,” Garcia wrote on X, making no secret of his plan to investigate Trump, his family, his staff and his appointees.

In an interview with Punchbowl News, Garcia teased investigation into alleged abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) under since-ousted Secretary Kristi Noem, corporate corruption, late convicted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein, and what Garcia called the “Trump crypto schemes,” as well as “the ‘Red Wedding’ of Don Jr.”
Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) similarly teased, “Subpoenas,” in a social media post.

Far-left candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) were projected to win at least five House races, expanding the number of avowed socialist lawmakers in the lower chamber from two to seven.

The DSA winners joining “Squad” socialists Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) in the House include: Melat Kiros of Colorado; Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania; Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, both of New York; and Donovan McKinney of Michigan.
Florida keeps right
On an otherwise difficult night, the results in the Sunshine State were one of the few outcomes the GOP can hang their hats on.
Incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) dispatched her socialist Democratic opponent Angie Nixon for the right to serve the remaining two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s Senate term.
In the governor’s race, Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) held off Democrat David Jolly by fewer than two percentage points, a narrower margin than many had expected.

“Florida sweeps again — congrats to the statewide ticket,” outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis wrote on X, noting Republican wins in the race to succeed him as well as in the contests for attorney general, agriculture commissioner and chief financial officer.

In a separate tweet, DeSantis boasted: “With the loss of governors races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, there will be only one state of the top ten most populous states with a Republican governor: Florida.”

articles.headline: US midterm elections 2026 live updates: Democrats win control of Congress as voters punish Trump

body: It’s 3am ET in Washington/8am GMT, and as people start seeing their phones ping with notifications, here are where things stand at the moment.

Democrats have won control of Congress in a stunning rebuke of Donald Trump’s agenda, delivering an astonishing result and a widely predicted “blue wave” across the country. As of now, Democrats have clinched 54 seats in the Senate (they needed 51 to reclaim the majority) and 225 House seats (they needed 218 to take control of the lower chamber). We’re still awaiting the results for several races – namely in Alaska.

There were several seismic and historic wins in federal and state races for Democrats. James Talarico became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; In Maine, progressive Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins after a thirty-year grip on the state’s US Senate seat; and Abdul El-Sayed won the US senate race in Michigan – one of the cycle’s most closely watched competitions.

We’re waiting on a number of nail-biting races to be called. The race for US Senate in Mississippi is extremely close, and could see a Democratic upset, and it’s still to early to call the Senate contest in Alaska.

Democrats also made history in a number of gubernatorial races.Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia means that she will be the first Black female governor in US history. Gina Hinojosa makes history as Texas’ first Latina governor, and the first Democrat to occupy the governor’s mansion since 1990. Meanwhile, David Crowley became Wisconsin’s first Black governor after winning his race tonight.

Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”

Fox News host Sean Hannity, one of Donald Trump’s most prominent supporters in conservative media, has acknowledged that the scale of public “hatred” towards the US president contributed to the Republicans’ heavy midtern election losses.
“Hatred is a hell of a motivator,” he told fellow panellist Harold Ford Jr.
He added: “I think the hatred for this man is unprecedented. I’ve never seen anything like it.”
In another historic first, the Democrats are projected to win Nevada’s second congressional district for the first time since its creation in 1981.
Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson is in the lead ahead of Republican David Flippo, although the race has not yet been called by the Associated Press.

If she holds on to that lead and flips the House seat, it will mark the first time since 1947 that Nevada has had an all-Democrat congressional delegation. Democrat incumbents have swept all of Nevada’s three remaining House seats, whose races have been called by AP.

“One of the biggest upsets in Nevada history, a district never held by a Democrat in its 45 years of existence,” said Jon Ralston, founder and CEO of the Nevada Independent, of Benitez-Thompson’s projected win.
Democrat James Talarico has won the US Senate race in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump.

Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and a staunch ally of the US president, in one of the most closely watched contests of the midterm elections to decide control of Congress.

“We just took back Texas!” the 37-year-old told jubilant supporters at an election night party in Austin, the state capital and his home city. “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We have just shown that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.”
Democrat Aaron Ford makes history as Nevada elects its first black governor
Nevada has elected Democrat Aaron Ford as its next governor, making him the first black person to hold the office in the state’s history.
His win toppled the Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo in a closely watched race, and delivered an important victory for the Democrats in one of the country’s key battleground states.
Ford ran his campaign with the backing of California governor Gavin Newsom and former vice-president Kamala Harris, focusing on the cost of living, housing affordability and student debt.
Opinion: The death knell of Trumpism has finally sounded
Moira Donegan

There’s a certain freedom in low expectations. Going in to Tuesday’s midterm elections, forecasts were so grim for the Republicans that poll watchers started trading a kind of knowing joke: that the results would either mean the end of the Trump era, or the end of the polling profession.

Amid those sorts of predictions, any Republican victories would have seemed like a minor miracle. The expectation was that Democrats would have a blowout; Republicans, counting on the final tally to be a bit more mixed, would therefore almost certainly have the freedom to claim that they’d done better than anyone had thought they would.
It will be difficult to credit those spins today. The electorate issued the president a message of dissatisfaction with the second Trump term, and voted decisively to curb his power.

Now, with a Senate majority, Democrats will be able to investigate the president and his cabinet members, draw public attention to their own agenda items, assert Congress’s constitutional prerogatives, and block Republican judicial appointments.

In the coming days and weeks, Trump will alternately say that the Republican losses were fake – the result of fraud by a nefarious but ill-defined conspiracy of Democrats and illegal immigrants – and that they were real, but somebody else’s fault.
His administration has signaled over the past weeks that it could make efforts to contest the certification of especially close Senate races, notably Alaska.

But the wind may have gone out of the sails of that plan for now: for what it’s worth, which isn’t much, Trump told the New York Times on Tuesday night that he would accept the results of the midterms. What’s certain is that he will rail into microphones and complain in all caps on social media. But it is not likely that any of that will go anywhere. Because Tuesday night – almost exactly 10 years after he won the presidency in an upset victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016 – the Trump era effectively came to an end.
'The American people sent a clear message,' says Obama
Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics.
In a statement on X, he said:
Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face.

These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country – including in areas once considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first.”

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.

“Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”

Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added: “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”
