articles.headline: ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
keyFacts: South Africans are voting in local municipal elections across nearly 300 municipalities amid reports of smooth voting, election officials said.
Analysts predict the ruling African National Congress party will lose further voter support due to anger over poor service delivery and corruption.
South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, giving parties 14 days to form governing structures.
body: - Published
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Election officials say voting is going smoothly, despite long queues at some polling stations.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.

For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.

The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.
We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.
They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.
But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change.
"We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.
Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.
On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.
The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.
The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision.
"It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.
Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.

Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.
The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.
South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.
Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity.
"Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.
Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".
These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.
Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.

A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.
Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention".

"If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.
The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.

Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.
The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done
Of South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.
But that might change.
Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC.
"And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.
Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.
One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.

The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.
DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.

The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".
She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".
Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.

These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.
Verwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.

Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.
Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.

The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.
The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.
Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.
A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.
Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros.
"We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.

Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa's elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline.

Ndou attributed this to the "calibre" of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns.
South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.

articles.headline: ‘Call me senator’: How Abdul El-Sayed beat Trump’s hate to create history
keyFacts: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won the Michigan US Senate election against Republican candidate Mike Rogers.
El-Sayed's victory makes him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
Vice President JD Vance is constitutionally obligated to swear El-Sayed into office in January.
body: Abdul El-Sayed had an uncomfortable message for US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance as he celebrated his historic election victory in Michigan.

They had used a range of racist labels and rhetoric to target El-Sayed ahead of the midterm elections, which he was contesting against Trump’s handpicked candidate, Mike Rogers. Trump mocked his name, and said that as president, he could call the Michigan physician and former public health official anything he wanted. Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist”, while Vance described him as a “psychopath”.
Now, the 42-year-old winner of the Michigan race pointed out, they would soon need to address him as a senator.

“JD, habibi [Arabic term of endearment], it is an irony – you are constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed told cheering supporters in the early hours of Wednesday, shortly after he was projected to win the highly contested race.
“Donald, I know you struggle with my name, so when JD swears me in, you can call me ‘senator.’ May we never have to see the likes of you in Michigan again.”

The Democrat’s victory over Republican Rogers on Tuesday made him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, following a campaign marked by attacks on his faith and criticism of his opposition to US military adventurism in the Middle East, and Washington’s support of Israel.
“To all the parents who struggled to explain why the president openly mocks someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost,” he said in his victory speech.
But beyond the historic significance of his election, El-Sayed focused on his promise to challenge economic inequality, healthcare and the cost of living in the country.
“Michigan, it just shouldn’t be this hard. It shouldn’t be this hard to buy a second bag of groceries or to fill your tank,” he said.
“It shouldn’t be this hard to pay your taxes and know that that money is going to be spent on you and your kids instead of dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids.”
The Muslim physician is set to win more than 52 percent of the vote with more than 95 percent of votes tallied.

His victory is seen as a breakthrough for progressives in the Democratic Party, who have increasingly challenged the party’s status quo over economic inequality and US wars abroad, including steadfast support for Israel.
Moreover, his win carries particular electoral significance, as Michigan is seen as a swing state that Trump won comfortably just two years ago.
Early life
El-Sayed was born and raised in the Detroit metropolitan area of Michigan and is of Egyptian descent.
He has often described his upbringing as that of a typical kid in a “brown” family of immigrants — he was expected to be high-achieving and successful at everything he did.

A physician and public health expert, he studied at the University of Michigan, where he was valedictorian of his 2007 graduating class. At his commencement, guest speaker and former President Bill Clinton praised the incoming senator for his speech focusing on inclusivity and equality.
“I wish every person in the world who believes that we are fated to have a clash of civilisations, and cannot reach across the religious divides, could have heard you speak today,” he said.
He went on to become a Rhodes Scholar at the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom. He also earned a medical degree from Columbia University in New York.
Before entering electoral politics, El-Sayed built his career in public health, working as an epidemiologist and eventually leading Detroit’s Health Department as its executive director.
He later became director of the Wayne County Department of Health, Human and Veteran Services.
The incoming senator is married to Indian-American psychiatrist Sarah Jukaku, with whom he has two daughters.
Start in politics
El-Sayed first sought elected office in 2018, when he ran for governor of Michigan on what many considered a progressive platform.
He campaigned on expanding healthcare access and challenging corporate influence but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer, who subsequently won the governorship.
Despite the defeat, the campaign helped establish El-Sayed as a prominent voice in Michigan politics.
Political positions
El-Sayed has advocated for universal healthcare, lower living costs and a foreign policy that prioritises domestic needs over military interventions abroad.
He supports Medicare for All, a government-funded universal healthcare programme that would expand coverage to all Americans.
The physician’s campaign has made healthcare affordability a central issue, arguing that access to medical treatment should not depend on a person’s income or employment status.
El-Sayed has also focused on rising grocery and fuel prices, criticising corporate influence over the economy and arguing that working families are struggling to afford everyday necessities.

On foreign policy, El-Sayed has been a vocal critic of US military involvement in the Middle East, opposing the US-Israeli war against Iran and calling for an end to American military assistance to Israel.
El-Sayed blamed the Iran war – which he has described as “stupid” – for higher gasoline prices and inflation, accusing the Trump administration of starting an unwarranted conflict.
He has also called out Israel’s government for committing genocide in Gaza, and argued that US taxpayer money should instead be directed towards education, healthcare and childcare.

“They tried to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” he said after declaring victory. “If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”
The Michigan-based politician has also criticised Trump’s trade war with Canada, arguing that tariffs have hurt his state’s economy, which is closely connected to its neighbour in the north.
Senate campaign
El-Sayed launched his Senate campaign in 2026, seeking to replace retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters in Michigan, a key battleground state.

In August, El-Sayed defeated Congresswoman Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary, delivering a significant victory for progressives and a setback for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which had backed his opponent openly.
Despite initially committing to support El-Sayed in the November election, Stevens endorsed Rogers days before the vote, drawing widespread criticism.
More than $50m was spent during the primary campaign, including at least $30m by AIPAC in support of Stevens.
Similar to his unsuccessful run for governor, his campaign focused on tackling the rising cost of living, expanding healthcare access and reducing corporate influence in Washington.
He also called for ending US military assistance to Israel, putting him at odds with sections of his own Democratic Party.
His campaign also faced Islamophobic attacks and accusations of anti-Semitism.
Following his primary victory, far-right commentators had seized on his use of the Arabic expression “inshallah”, meaning “God willing”, to portray him as a religious threat to the United States.
Trump accused El-Sayed of hating Jews and Israel, while his Republican opponent, Rogers, alleged that he had sympathies and links to the Muslim Brotherhood.

In the last televised debate in October, Rogers suggested El-Sayed had the same supporters as groups like Hamas, implying his platform was a threat to “national security”. El-Sayed vehemently denied the allegations.
On Wednesday, he hit back at those who had tried to weaponise his faith and ethnicity against him.

“We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid, or genocide, or war,” El-Sayed said. Until now, he said, his campaign had used “inshallah” to emphasise their hopes for victory. “But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into alhamdulillah [praise be to God].”

articles.headline: WoW: Forever's massive pre-launch balance patch breaks from the chains Classic power, increasing 'the health of higher level creatures to compensate'
keyFacts: Developers announced that the WoW: Forever pre-launch patch increases class damage and raises higher-level creature health to compensate.
The update significantly boosts tank threat generation and introduces new abilities like the rogue Shank skill.
Developers stated they will conduct a large tuning pass based on player data once players engage in content past level 30.
body: "Over the course of Beta, we came to the realization that trying to hold ourselves roughly to Classic power budgets for each class meant that every new element we added needed to come at the expense of something else. Those reductions left some iconic abilities feeling lackluster, and closed the door to other potentially exciting design options."

"So over the last two weeks, we’ve raised damage on classes across the game, and have increased the health of higher level creatures to compensate. This additional 'headroom' has allowed us to tune things to a place that we hope feels better overall," via the official WoW forums.

This honestly makes the most sense to me—yes, there are some elements of Classic I want WoW: Forever to preserve. The slower, more relaxed pace and the time-to-kill (something that has been maintained to a deliberate, intentional degree) of oldschool MMOs, for one.

But if you're gonna do Classic+, you shouldn't have to limit yourself to the power and ability budgets that came out 20 years ago. You might as well go whole-hog and try to get things feeling a little more interesting, if still along the lines of that vanilla feeling.

The statement linked above, which was posted in a series of pre-release patch notes, continues: "Beyond that, some of this round of changes reflects areas where we were likely hasty in turning to Burning Crusade or Wrath-era solutions rather than carving out new ones that better fit into the Forever combat model.

"Our aim in class design is not perfect numerical equality, but rather for every class to feel valuable to the groups they join, with powerful, unforgettable moments brought on by mastering them. In Forever this is accomplished by doubling down on the strengths and differences that make each class unique, rather than overly unifying them."

Hear hear! Homogenisation is the death of interesting class design, and I've certainly played MMOs where that's been a massive problem (I am very much hoping that FF14's Evolved job reworks hit this mark). The patch notes themselves are interesting, too.

For starters, tanks have had their threat bonuses absolutely ramped. Warriors' defensive stance has spiked from a 30% to an 80% increase and Druid's bear form has been bumped from 50% to 115%, with similar threat generation buffs for Paladins. This is primarily to offset the removal of Blessing of Salvation, which seems smart to me—you probably shouldn't be balancing threat generation writ large over the spell of one class.

Rogues now have an ability called "Shank", an off-hand weapon energy generation tool—which has a different flavour for each specialisation. Combat rogues get more energy from it, Subtlety rogues can get extra combo points, and Assassination rogues can use it to debuff enemies to make them more vulnerable to their poisons.

This is just skimming the top of the iceberg—there have been a ton of changes: "We’ve used the data and feedback gathered during Beta testing to get everything tuned to a reasonable place. However, the only true test of that tuning is the game itself. With the exception of bugs and serious outliers, we don’t plan on making big tuning changes between now and the opening of the raids next month.

"Once we have sufficient data from players leveling past 30 and engaging in a wide range of content, we expect that we will do a large tuning pass based on our data. And this is all merely a starting point for the classes in Forever, which will continue to evolve over the course of the months and years ahead just as they did following the original launch in 2004."
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Harvey's history with games started when he first begged his parents for a World of Warcraft subscription aged 12, though he's since been cursed with Final Fantasy 14-brain and a huge crush on G'raha Tia. He made his start as a freelancer, writing for websites like Techradar, The Escapist, Dicebreaker, The Gamer, Into the Spine—and of course, PC Gamer. He'll sink his teeth into anything that looks interesting, though he has a soft spot for RPGs, soulslikes, roguelikes, deckbuilders, MMOs, and weird indie titles. He also plays a shelf load of TTRPGs in his offline time. Don't ask him what his favourite system is, he has too many.

articles.headline: US midterms: Democrats win House and Senate from Republicans
keyFacts: Democratic Party candidates have secured control of both the US Senate and the House of Representatives in the midterm elections.
The election results included several historic firsts, such as Abdul El-Sayed becoming the first Muslim US senator by winning in Michigan.
International leaders and officials responded to the outcome, with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa stating it could introduce a new era in world relations.
body: What you need to know
- Democratic Party candidates secure control of the US Senate and House of Representatives
- Trump says Democrats 'did a good job' in midterm elections
- Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race to become first Muslim senator in US history
- James Talarico wins Democrats' first Senate seat in Texas in decades
- Annie Andrews stuns Republicans in South Carolina
- Democrats also notch wins in gubernatorial contests in Ohio and Georgia
Follow the latest developments from the US midterm elections:
Live election results
AfD's Weidel attributes Republicans defeats to Iran war's 'considerable consequences'

German right-wing populist AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel told the "t-online" news website that while midterm losses for parties in power were the norm in the US, "the extent of the Republican defeat is notable and can be best explained with the considerable consequences of the Iran war."
She said one frequent and loud campaign promise from 2016, 2020 and 2024 had come back home to roost in 2026.
"Trump promised his voters not to conduct and interventionist foreign policy," she said. "This broken promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans."
Weidel said it was in both Europe's and Germany's interests to bring the war in Iran — but also the war in Ukraine — to an end as quickly as possible.

The politician, whose party tends to be quite closely aligned with Trump's MAGA movement and some of its core backers like Elon Musk, has made no public social media comments on the vote. Instead, her comments to "t-online" focused mainly on public protests over the weekend in some cities, which she linked to "militant left-wing extremists, migrant mobs, and organized crime families."
Iran's Qalibaf says US voters said 'no to war'

The speaker of Iran's parliament, Mohammad Qalibaf, who is also the country's chief negotiator in the stalled talks with the US and intermediaries, has celebrated the result online — saying that whatever the main motivator, US voters had ultimately spoken out against the war in the Middle East.

"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," he wrote on social media. "If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."
He did not elaborate on this vague threat, after several tense months of relative inactivity in the military and diplomatic standoff.
Meanwhile, a written statement was published on the website of Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei saying that anybody expecting a shift in US policy after the vote was "seriously mistaken."

"Those who still harbor even the slightest hope that the behavior of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken," the statement said.

Khamenei was severely wounded in the US strikes at the start of the war that killed his father and much of his family. He has not been seen or heard in public since amid conflicting reports about his medical and physical status, but written statements attributed to him appear periodically.
China calls vote an 'internal matter,' Russia says it won't impact Ukraine stance
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters the midterm elections were an "internal matter" for the US.
She said Beijing remained willing to work with the US to implement agreements reached between the two countries' leaders, strengthen communication and manage differences appropriately.

Chinese President Xi Jinping made a high-profile state visit to the US to meet with Donald Trump amid this year's UN General Assembly, which he did not attend. While the pair tried to put on an amicable show, very little of substance emerged from the visit beyond an agreement to extend a temporary tariff truce in their trade spat for a few more weeks.
There has also been speculation about a possible trialteral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, but for now nothing has been formally arranged or announced.
In Moscow, meanwhile, state news agency RIA cited Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov as saying he planned to wait for the final results.

"The Democratic Party leadership's approach to relations with Russia is sharply negative. There is nothing new about that," Ryabkov said. He said it would not impact Russia's position regarding its invasion of Ukraine, as the Trump administration continues to push for peace talks, albeit only arranging working-level negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv as yet.

"Our principled and consistent line regarding Ukraine — as well as our foreign policy in general — is not based on short-term considerations, and, naturally, does not depend on the fluctuations of the political barometer in other countries," Ryabkov said.
A night of historic firsts in US elections
Tuesday night not only ushered in a series of changes in the US Congress, but it also saw a number of historic firsts in elections across the country.

Abdul El-Sayed will become the first Muslim US senator when he is sworn in next January after winning in Michigan. His win came nearly 20 years after the election of Keith Ellison to the House of Representatives. Ellison was the first Muslim elected to that body.
After defeating Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy, Amy Acton is set to become the first female governor of Ohio.
In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black female governor of any state, as well as Georgia's first black governor, by beating billionaire Rick Jackson.

Another historic gubernatorial race took place in New Mexico, where Deb Haaland became the first Indigenous American elected to that state's highest office. Haaland is a member of the Laguna Pueblo tribe and was US secretary of the interior under former President Joe Biden.

At the same time, Ojibwe lawmaker Peggy Flanagan became the first Indigenous woman elected to the US Senate. After years in public service at the state level, she wil now represent Minnesota in Washington.

And in New Hampshire, Chris Pappas was also elected to the Senate, where he will be the first openly gay man to serve. In Alabama, Allison Montgomery became the first transperson elected to the state legislature, beating a Republican who repeatedly verbally attacked her for being trans.

More history is likely to be made in January if Hakeem Jeffries, considered the current frontrunner as minority leader, becomes speaker of the House of Representatives, as he would be the first Black man to hold that position.
European politicians react to the 'powerful political signal' out of US

Left-leaning Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has repeatedly clashed with Donald Trump in the past year and who faces snap elections himself at the end of the month, said that American society "voted against the policies that only impoverish," such as hate, machismo, climate denialism and the privileges of the elites.
He drew parallels to Brazil's presidential election and the early vote he called, facing a legislative deadlock with his minority government, in Spain.

"It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain," Sanchez wrote. "The ultra wave that [Alberto Nunez] Feijoo and [Santiago] Abascal are trying to ride is no longer growing: it is crumbling."

French Finance Minister Roland Lescure reminded BFM TV that even after losing control of Congress, Trump would remain in charge on the vast majority of US foreign policy issues, and seemed to warn that the president might not prove the type to favor compromise and collaboration.

Lescure said, "Either he decides to rise above the fray, acknowledging that changes are necessary," particularly on issues like gasoline prices and his foreign policy, "or he does not." Lescure said this would be something "we will need to keep an eye on in the coming days."

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store told Reuters news agency it was a "powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters." He said voices were emerging in US politics that "are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy."

The co-leader of Germany's Green Party, Franziska Brantner, said the result was a "stop sign towards Trump and his billionaires." She said that while this pointed to "hope" for the US democratic system "hopefully getting back on its feet," it was too soon to breathe a sigh of relief in the European Union.

"On the contrary, we must really bet on Europe and on our own strengths," Brantner said. She said Trump had made it clear that he did not respect the EU and wanted to divide it, and that he wanted less and less to do with supporting Ukraine. "That means, we have our own responsibility for ourselves, no matter what the final result."
Christel Schaldemose, a European Parliament vice president from Denmark, said she was "cautiously optimistic" on Europe's behalf.

"Not because everything will now change for the better, but because it could benefit support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world," she said. But she also added that the EU must continue its course of standing on its own two feet, saying "that's not up for debate."
Ramaphosa sees 'new era' after Democratic wins
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the Democratic sweep of Congress could usher in a "new era in world relations" after voters dealt President Donald Trump a major electoral setback.

"The Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken," Ramaphosa told reporters. "I do think that this is going to introduce a new era in world relations."

Relations between the US and South Africa have deteriorated under Trump. During a televised Oval Office meeting in May 2025, he confronted Ramaphosa with misleading footage and news clippings promoting false claims of a genocide against white South Africans. Ramaphosa repeatedly sought to rebut the allegations.

The Trump administration has also cut aid, expelled South Africa's ambassador and, this week, moved to end its duty-free access to the US market under the African Growth and Opportunity Act from January.
Ramaphosa said South Africa would continue trading with the US while seeking new export markets.
"Diversification has now become the order of the day," he said.
WATCH: Sweeping Democrat wins deliver rebuke to Trump
Democrats have scored stunning victories in states long considered Republican strongholds, flipping key Senate seats.
Brandon Bohrn, a US political analyst with the Bertelsmann Stiftung, analyzes the election results for DW.
RECAP — Democrats claim control of Congress, flipping several Senate seats

Welcome to our coverage of the US midterm elections, particularly if you're outside US time zones and were tucked up in bed as the poll-closing drama unfolded overnight. Here's the lay of the land stateside in what's now the early hours of the morning-after the vote which many saw as a referendum on President Donald Trump.

The Democrats have fared better than polls predicted, at least based on what should now be reliable projections. They have comfortably taken control of the House of Representatives and claimed a majority in the upper chamber of Congress, the Senate.

In a major blow for the Donald Trump administration, they have swung at least seven of the 35 Senate seats up for grabs — in North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine. Some of those states were Republican-held for decades; Kansas' two Senate seats had been reliably Republican since before World War II.

Counting in the House races is slower, with all 435 seats up for grabs, but the Democrats have already passed the post to win the majority of the chamber with the better part of 100 seats yet to be called.

These results should markedly strengthen the Democrats' hand in Congress, giving them the power to block legislation (if perhaps not executive orders directly from President Donald Trump) and launch investigations into Trump's administration. In the Senate, they will be able to block his appointees as judges or for senior roles in government.
Trump himself praised the Democrats in an interview on Fox News on election night, saying he thought they did a "good job" and "fought hard."
"I don't view it as a hit on me," he said, despite having urged voters to act as if his name was on the midterm ballots during the campaign.
Democrats claim majority of US governorships
Democrats have won a majority of US governorships for the first time in two decades, capturing offices long held by Republicans in Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Georgia.
The gains give the party more power at the state level to challenge President Donald Trump's policies on immigration, voting rules and the deployment of National Guard troops.
Several victories have also made history:
- Georgia: Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms has become the first Black woman elected governor in the US, defeating Republican billionaire Rick Jackson
- Texas: Gina Hinojosa has defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott to become the state's first Latina governor, despite being outspent five-to-one on advertising
- New Mexico: Deb Haaland, a former US interior secretary, has become the first Native American woman elected governor

In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton defeated biotech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, describing it as "the honor of my lifetime." The victory came after a bitter campaign in which Ramaswamy's use of Acton's estranged mother in an attack ad drew widespread criticism.

In Iowa, state auditor Rob Sand thanked voters for his victory over Republican Zach Lahn. Preliminary results put Sand around 12 percentage points ahead in a state Trump won by roughly 13 points in 2024.
Republicans have held Florida, where Congressman Byron Donalds defeated David Jolly, a former Republican who ran as a Democrat.

The results could also shape the next presidential election. Governors influence election administration, while three Democrats considered potential presidential contenders in 2028 — Pennsylvania's Josh Shapiro, Illinois' JB Pritzker and Maryland's Wes Moore — have won reelection.
DW Washington bureau chief: Results are 'more than a setback' for Republicans
The midterm election results are "more than a setback" for Republicans and President Donald Trump, DW's Washington bureau chief Ines Pohl said.
The results represent "a dramatic loss of political power" for Trump's Republican Party, she said.
See her full analysis here:
WATCH: Republicans react to historic defeat in Texas Senate race

DW spoke to Republican supporters at an election watch party in Austin, Texas, after Democrat James Talarico won the Senate race in the state, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold.
German leaders congratulate Democrats, stress foreign policy power remains with the Trump administration

Metin Hakverdi, who serves as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coordinator of transatlantic cooperation, said he expects the US midterm results to significantly impact the political situation between Berlin and Washington.
"America has chosen change," he told news agency DPA, while stressing that Trump remains largely in charge of foreign policy and that Germany will continue to reach out to both parties.

"We must especially not limit our contacts to individual political camps," he added, while also highlighting the historic significance of the first Indigenous woman being elected governor of New Mexico and the first black woman as governor of Georgia.
Hakverdi, a Social Democrat, has extended family in the United States and attended high school there.

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated Democrats on what he called their "historic victory." He also emphasized that the White House will remain the same and Berlin will continue to cooperate with it.
WATCH: DW covers the US midterm results live
Here you can catch DW's live video coverage of the results and reactions to Democrats flipping both houses of the US Congress, as well as several governors' seats:
Mood on the ground at an election-night watch party in Detroit
The mood was cheery at the Michigan Democrats' headquarters in Detroit as it became increasingly clear that progressive Abdul El-Sayed was going to win his Senate race.
Crowds gathered at a watch party in Detroit's Eastern Market as results from across the country were projected on a big screen.
Cheers erupted from between the music for every Democratic win.
Attendees voiced surprise that the Democratic Party had already achieved a majority in the Senate without having called the state of Michigan yet.
Others shared concerns about President Trump's repeated announcements to make use of his veto power in response to the Democrats’ majority.

articles.headline: Iran says U.S. election results show Americans reject the war
keyFacts: Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday that U.S. midterm election results showed Americans reject the war launched against his country.
President Trump stated Tuesday night that he has no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran despite ongoing attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.
Four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Wednesday.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday that the U.S. midterm election results reflected Americans' rejection of President Trump launched against his country. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf added a warning that if Mr. Trump does not heed the message from American voters, it will bring "a Nightmare."

- President Trump acknowledged Tuesday night that the war with Iran was partially to blame for the GOP's resounding midterm elections losses. But Mr. Trump told The Wall Street Journal he didn't regret the conflict and added he "would have done it again."

- Despite signs of a to reach a peace deal, ships continue to come under attack in the Strait of Hormuz. Four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while transiting the waterway, Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Wednesday.
Trump says U.S. has no immediate plan to strike Iran, despite being "locked and loaded"

President Trump told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday evening that he had no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran, after keeping the option on the table for weeks ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

"We seem to be getting everything we want," the FT quoted Mr. Trump as saying, referring to the current stalemate with Iran. While major fighting stopped weeks ago, the standoff has seen the Islamic Republic continue threatening and attacking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, which in turn has kept global oil prices 60% to 70% higher than they were before the war started, driving up consumer costs across the globe.
Asked whether there would be a new attack on Iran later this week, Mr. Trump said "we're locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it."

Despite the impasse, the president claimed the current circumstances were "brilliant," with oil still reaching global markets from the Persian Gulf, including under U.S. military escort through the Strait of Hormuz.
"If you think about it, we haven't really had a war with them in a long time. Six months, maybe more," asserted Mr. Trump.
China says avoiding more conflict in Middle East a "top priority"
China's foreign ministry said Wednesday that avoiding a resumption of the conflict between Iran and the U.S. was a "top priority" in its diplomatic efforts in the region.

"The top priority is to avoid the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East that would bring disaster to the region's people," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing.

China will "support Iran and the U.S. in resolving disputes through negotiations, promote finding a political settlement to the Yemen issue, to help reach a proper and comprehensive solution for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz," she added.
China is an economic ally of Iran. Chinese purchases of Iranian crude oil amount to nearly 45% of the Iranian government's budget, according to a U.S. government report from March 2025.
Later this month, Beijing will send its Middle East envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia for visits "aimed at promoting peace talks (and) easing tensions," the foreign ministry said Wednesday.
CBS/AFP
Lebanese prime minister warns of "risks of renewed war," and of Lebanon being dragged in again

In a message seemingly directed at the Iran-backed group Hezbollah, Lebanon's prime minister warned Wednesday against any moves that could pull the country into renewed fighting between Iran and the U.S. and Israel.

"Faced with the risks of renewed war in the region, I renew my warning of the dangers of dragging Lebanon into a new senseless adventure in service of outside interests," Nawaf Salam said on Wednesday, without explicitly mentioning Hezbollah.

Southern Lebanon has been a major front in the interlinked regional conflicts, with fighting between Iran's Hezbollah allies and Israel's military driving tens of thousands of people from their homes and killing almost 9,000 since Oct. 7, 2023, according to the Lebanese health ministry.

Hezbollah, long a powerful political and paramilitary force in the country, pulled Lebanon directly into the war with Israel by launching strikes on the Jewish state in support of Hamas after the 2023 terror attacks sparked the war in Gaza, and then by firing rockets and missiles in support of Iran after joint U.S.-Israeli strikes commenced on Feb. 28.

The Lebanon conflict has proven to be a major sticking point in negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, as Tehran has consistently rejected any peace deal with Washington that does not also end fighting in Lebanon and Gaza.

A fragile ceasefire agreement reached between Israel and Hezbollah in June has halted most large-scale fighting between the two sides, but Israeli forces still occupy a large section of southern Lebanon, and there are sporadic attacks by both sides.
"We do not accept the country again becoming a theater for the conflict of others," Salam added, saying Lebanon had "already paid a heavy price."

President Trump threatened repeatedly ahead of the U.S. midterm elections to renew strikes on Iran, but he told the Financial Times as the results came in Tuesday evening that he had no immediate plans to order attacks.
CBS/AFP
Four tankers catch fire while transiting Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military says
Four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military said Wednesday, after it warned no one would benefit from a return to war.

"Four non-compliant oil tankers attempting to pass through the prohibited passage south of the Strait of Hormuz were destroyed after striking naval mines and are still burning," Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement quoted by state TV.
"Two other non-compliant ships or vessels have also been halted," they said
The attacks come even as a diplomatic push is underway aimed at reaching a deal between the U.S. and Iran. Indirect talks via Qatari, Pakistani and Saudi mediators are understood to be underway.

Although both sides previously expressed some hope of reaching an agreement, Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council on Tuesday cast doubt on progress toward a deal, calling the U.S. response to their demands "not convincing."
CBS/AFP
Iran says midterm results reflect rejection of war
Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday the midterm election results mean Americans have rejected the war with his country.
"Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a post on X.
He cited the increased cost of living or "conscience" as two of the possible reasons for the widespread Republican losses in Tuesday's vote.
"If the U.S. govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," Ghalibaf added.
Trump acknowledges war with Iran partially to blame for GOP's election defeat
President Trump acknowledged on Tuesday night that the war with Iran was partially responsible for the Republicans' defeat in the midterm elections.
In a phone interview with Fox News, Mr. Trump said "part of it was Iran" when explaining the result of the elections, but that "at the same time, people understand the importance of what I've done."
In a separate interview with the The Wall Street Journal, the president reiterated his comments and added that he does not regret starting the war with Tehran.
"I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again," he told the newspaper.
Qatar is said to expect feedback from U.S. and Iran on latest peace proposal within 36 hours

Qatari mediators expect feedback within 36 hours from Iranian and U.S. negotiators on new ideas aimed at getting both sides closer to a deal to end the war, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing an official briefed on the talks.
"The mediators came up with a new suggestion to move the process along, and it's currently being studied by the two sides," the official told Reuters.

Efforts to reach a deal to prevent a return to fighting between Iran and the U.S. have ramped up recently. President Trump has said he is still open to an agreement, but has also threatened to resume major U.S. strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S.
On the eve of the elections, Mr. Trump again expressed hope that an agreement could still be reached, claiming Tehran wanted a settlement "as soon as possible."
Iranian officials declared Monday that the ball "is in the U.S. court" and they said Iran's core demands to end the war would not be altered.

articles.headline: Apple Music's upcoming feature will let you record yourself doing karaoke
keyFacts: Apple Music is introducing a new karaoke video recording feature called Selfie Sing.
MacRumors reports that the feature will launch with iOS 27.3, which is currently available in beta.
Users can record videos, apply voice effects, and share their performances, though the feature uses a specific playlist rather than the full catalog.
body: Apple Music's upcoming feature will let you record yourself doing karaoke
Selfie Sing will roll out with iOS 27.3.

Apple Music will introduce a new feature that will give you a way to record yourself singing karaoke without having to use another app. It first introduced a karaoke functionality called "Sing" that lets you take over the vocals of songs back in 2022. As MacRumors reports, this is sort of an upgraded version of that called "Selfie Sing," and it will launch with iOS 27.3, which is now available in beta. It will let you record videos of yourself singing to music while the lyrics to the songs scrolls up on the screen in real time. The feature comes with its own playlist, however, and isn't supported by the service's whole catalog.

"There are some songs everyone knows by heart, the ones that come on and suddenly the whole room's singing along," the company wrote in its description of Selfie Sing. "This playlist is loaded with them, each one ready to become your next Selfie Sing." The playlist, so far, includes Since U Been Gone by Kelly Clarkson, What Makes You Beautiful by One Direction, Like a Virgin by Madonna, Baby One More Time by Britney Spears and 9 to 5 by Dolly Parton.

Just choose a song and then enable the camera to start recording. You can add effects to your voice or change its volume — your options include Megaphone, Echo, Concert Hall and Studio — if you wish before saving or sharing the video with your friends. Apple has just rolled out iOS 27.3 beta for download, and it will bring more Siri AI features and a redesigned Health app to your iPhones, as well. The new mobile OS expected to be widely available sometime this December.

articles.headline: The Switch 2 Zelda: Ocarina of Time Is a Brilliant Remake
keyFacts: Nintendo released a 60 dollar Ocarina of Time remake exclusive to the Switch 2 featuring completely redone graphics and improved controls.
The reviewer stated that the remake features enhanced visual splendor surpassing Breath of the Wild while keeping the original story and scale.
The author noted that some areas, dialogue, and weapon locations differ from the 1998 original version.
body: It was way back in 1998 when I finished Ocarina of Time. I remember how incredible it all was, not only to play but also to look at. N64 games back then felt stunning — so impressive that I rushed out to make the N64 the first Nintendo home console I ever owned.

Those days are gone, and N64 games now look pretty rough to my eyes. But with the $60 Ocarina of Time remake, exclusive to the Switch 2, Nintendo brings some of that magic back again; I’ve never had more fun replaying a game in my life.

When I first tried the new version of Ocarina for about an hour a few weeks ago, it felt like it was replacing my old memories of playing the original game. More than a week into playing at home, I can confirm that the remake has completely replaced my memories of the original. I’ve revisited the N64 version a few times through the Switch Online N64 app, but it feels so minimal and awkward compared with the remake that now I can’t go back.
More from CNET
A whole new version of the familiar

Everything in Ocarina of Time has been created fresh again. Like some sort of setbuilder making all the pieces of an old show from memory, it’s astonishing how Ocarina is an old game made with completely redone graphics. It outdoes Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom in visual splendor, with similarly gorgeous open vistas at every turn.

Just as Ocarina of Time inspired Breath of the Wild, it’s Breath of the Wild that’s now reshaped Ocarina — at least, visually. The scope, story and challenges in Ocarina remain just about the same, creating a more intimate experience despite its sense of epic scale. If you’ve never played it before, think of it as a theme park version of the supersized Hyrule in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

But I appreciate its more contained scale even more now. I got lost in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, and not always in a good way. To be honest, at times, parts of those games began to feel repetitive. Ocarina of Time’s story is told more directly, with clearly laid-out goals and a faster pace. It feels like a true fusion of the sandbox-like open worlds of recent Zelda games and the intricate, puzzle-driven storylines of older ones.
The improved controls are phenomenal

I’d love this new Ocarina even if it only brought updated graphics, reworked sound and new voice acting, which grew on me. But its control scheme makes the game far more intuitive to play. The old Ocarina didn’t have a jump button: Link just auto-jumped! Here, you can jump anywhere. The old game never had a second analog stick to control your viewing angle: It relied on “Z-targeting” to look ahead or to recenter your focus on objects and enemies. Now, you can look around and Z-target with a trigger button — something that modern Zelda players probably just take for granted.

Some areas are different now: Early on in Kokiri Forest, the way you find the first sword is different. The dialogue has also changed. That’s just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the many little shifts here, which become hard to notice. At some point, my experience of the new 2026 version simply took over and overwrote all my old, fuzzy memories of the 1998 version. It’s now, once again, the game as it felt to me back then.
The story is enchanting me again

Maybe it’s that I’m getting older, or I don’t replay games such as Ocarina of Time year after year like some do, but I realize I forgot a lot of what happens in this game. But I look forward to every night I get a chance to play it again. It’s that good.

I didn’t think that would happen, not with RPGs and Zelda games advancing so much over the years. It’s a testament to Ocarina of Time that its structure and mystery still feel perfectly paced. There are tons of side missions, but the main story arc is strong and continuous. I felt a sense of awe more than once, even when it came to things I knew would happen. The time travel — which I hope doesn’t spoil too much for anyone who’s never played before, though, hey, it is called Ocarina of Time — still feels wondrous.

I was skeptical about Nintendo spending all its resources updating classic games over the last year or so — a trend that started with Starfox, continued with Switch Sports Resort and has returned here. I wanted new games for the Switch 2 — not retreads. But I have to admit that Nintendo has done these remakes with expert care. And in the case of Ocarina of Time, the effort truly feels like it transcends the original. As much as I ended up loving Star Fox again, it never felt as much like a new game as this Ocarina remake does.

Is it a truly new game? No. But it feels like the most singular Zelda game again, taking precedence even over Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. And with its graphic overhaul, it now feels like a cousin to those games in a new way, a sort of trilogy (but not exactly). I find myself, once again, appreciating how absurd and adorable all the characters are. Zelda games have such a goofy sense of humor, and I feel like Ocarina does more than Breath and Tears do. I’ve gotten a kick out of finding every side character in Hyrule just to see their new faces.
And the dungeons in Ocarina of Time are so good. I want Zelda games to return to the kind of intricate, puzzle-filled dungeons found here.
Please, may have I some Majora?
I’m so stunned by how much I love the new Ocarina that I’m wondering what other magic Nintendo could work on other throwbacks. Do this for Mario 64, or Pilotwings.
Or…Majora’s Mask.

The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask is the “other” Zelda game for N64, and it’s even more brilliantly conceived. Remaking it for the Switch 2 now seems like a when — not an if — considering Ocarina’s Hyrule has been completely rebuilt with new graphics. Nintendo brought Ocarina and Majora to 3DS, and the cycle could repeat again here. I’d be all for it.

Could this all be a massive test run for a future Zelda that doesn’t exist yet? It certainly feels like it — but when? The remastered version of Metroid Prime paved the way for Metroid Prime 4’s release. Beyond the battle-focused Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment, this is the first Zelda game made exclusively with the Switch 2’s hardware in mind — and its lush visuals show it. It’s the best-looking game on the Switch 2 yet, and of course it makes me wonder what a new Zelda game could feel like. Or heck, a new Mario.

This reconstruction of Ocarina of Time feels like it’s strutting, dripping with luxury, full of glorious style, a symphony played with a full orchestra. And somehow, unleashing it all in service of a fantastic remake doesn’t feel excessive. I’m having a blast playing it, but I also want to see what this opens up for the next generation of Nintendo Switch 2 games.
But if you’ve never played a Zelda game before and have a Switch 2, I envy you: The new Ocarina of Time is an incredible place to start.

articles.headline: Achieving nirvana: Enlightenment 0.28 hits the desktop
keyFacts: Enlightenment version 0.28 has been released as the latest update for the long-standing Linux graphical environment.
The new Enlightenment release includes 68 lines of changes, adding features such as Pipewire audio support and preliminary NetBSD compatibility.
The Trinity Desktop Environment project announced release 14.1.7, featuring bug fixes and taskbar updates for the KDE 3 port.
body: Fresh on the desktop this week is a new version of Enlightenment as well the continuation of noughties hero KDE 3, the Trinity Desktop Environment, for those who prefer things a little old school.

Enlightenment version 0.28 is the latest release of one of the older Linux graphical environments, which first appeared in 1997. Version 0.28 arrives nearly two years after the previous release – we reported on Enlightement 0.27 in January 2025. If you're not familiar with this venerable window manager, often referred to as just E, we refer you back to that article, which also explains Enlightenment's slightly strange version numbering scheme.

Last time around we noted that its single-line release notes really didn't give us much to write about. The development team has made up for it this time, with some 68 lines of changes. It's both the same old E, and simultaneously a modern tool: it is still an X11 window manager, but it can also act as a Wayland compositor if you prefer. It offers conventional stacking resizable windows, but also can act as a tiling window manager if you prefer. On recent distros, it can now talk to the Pipewire audio server, and it can also work with NetworkManager to control network connections. This version delivers preliminary support for NetBSD too.

This isn't really a tool for newbies or those looking for a simple easy desktop. A sign of its age is that the first-run wizard asks if you want windows to activate as soon as you move the mouse pointer over them. This was traditional 20th century Unix behavior, and in the early days of Linux it was called "focus-follows-mouse," but it's rarely seen today. E isn't a full desktop environment: it only offers a few of its own optional tools, such as the Ecrire text editor, Ephoto picture viewer, Evisum task manager, and Rage video player. Even its taskbar is optional. It is more like a basis for experienced users to customize and build their own environment around.
Trinity is back

The Trinity Desktop Environment has a rather lower learning curve: TDE is a port of the final version of KDE 3 to modern Linux. Proving old school is still cool, the project – which keeps the look and feel of 2005-era KDE 3.5 alive – has just announced TDE release 14.1.7 , with dozens of bug fixes and plenty of new features. Among these is a tweak to the kicker/taskbar: you can now scroll the taskbar using the mouse wheel, flicking through your open applications.This release drops support for Ubuntu 24.10 "Oracular Oriole" but adds support for the latest 26.10 "Stonking Stingray."

Forks of older versions by users disenchanted with new versions are a recurring feature of the FOSS world, but they often tend to peter out after a while. TDE is one of the exceptions: we first reported on a new release in 2021 and again in 2023 . ®

articles.headline: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) review
keyFacts: Eurogamer reviewed Nintendo's new remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, nearly thirty years after the original game's release.
The remake features modern graphics, a dual-thumbstick camera system, and user-interface tweaks like a jump button and a trigger mini-menu for items.
The reviewer stated that the gameplay updates improve the pace and flow of challenging areas like the Water Temple without altering meaningful original elements.
body: I have a friend who first played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time back in the day, when the game was only just released and he was home from university for Christmas. This is objectively the best of all times to play any video game: not Christmas specifically, but dropped out of the regular world and faced with a few weeks filled with nothing pressing to do whatsoever. Years later, though, my friend told me that the magic of the game didn't just come down to the playing of it, but the way that the playing of it unfolded.

Here's what he meant. He'd play all day, curtains drawn, family ignored, working through dungeons and pelting across Hyrule Field on Epona. Then in the evening he'd call his girlfriend, who was back with her own family for Christmas. She always wanted to know what he'd got up to that day. And not in East Sussex; she wanted to know what he'd got up to in Hyrule.

So as he played he took regular breaks to tell someone else about what he had encountered, and what he had discovered, and what he had yet to overcome. It is my bright delight today to be able to tell you that, around thirty years later, having just revisited the game in Nintendo's new remake, Ocarina of Time is still worth telling people about. It's still an adventure so surprising, so satisfying, so moving that I need to talk about it.

Here's the thing, though. Despite the game being a cast-iron masterpiece, this reaction was something of a surprise to me. Or rather, it was a surprise precisely because the game was a cast-iron masterpiece. In truth, a couple of weeks ago I wasn't really aching to head back to Ocarina of Time after all these years. I kind of dreaded having to slog through an echoing, once-great game and summon a thousand words of measured reverence afterwards.

Thankfully I had forgotten two things. The first is that I am an idiot, which means that I had failed to realise that any chance to replay a Zelda should be leapt at. And secondly, it turns out that I'd forgotten exactly what kind of masterpiece Ocarina of Time is. And along with that last point - and we'll get to this properly in a bit - I hadn't realised that there's a secret ingredient to this specific remake that has proved absolutely essential to its greatness, and that has nothing at all to do with the code running on the Switch 2.

Let's deal with remake duties here. This is more or less the game that people played back in 1998. The beats of the adventure, with Link travelling between different eras of Hyrule in order to defeat Ganon, remain the same. You still start in Kokiri Forest and you still ride Epona over the fence at Lon Lon Ranch in one of the great heart-racing, skin-prickling moments in all of art. If you're stuck in a dungeon, you can almost always use an existing guide from the N64 game to work your way through it. The game world is still broken up into little chunks that fade out and in as you move between them. And each game still begins with that unskippably evocative intro that has Link and Epona dashing over a misty hill with the moon behind them, Zelda meets Susan Cooper.

Changes though? For one thing the whole game's been updated with modern graphics, and has ditched any and all fixed cameras for a modern system of movement on one thumbstick and camera on the other. One example: Hyrule Castle Town, in my memory at least, always had a central camera and you would pivot about its streets as if you were a horse on a circus merry-go-round.

Now it's pure Frozen territory, cobbled paths racing off in every direction and you can explore them with the camera rushing behind you. The game's spaces feel less like elaborate machines that you were a mechanical part of, and more like video game spaces. Yes, from the way I've phrased that I now see that something of a trade-off has taken place here. I loved that sense you got in early 3D games that the whole thing was a clever practical trick that was forever almost about to collapse in on itself, but anyway! The new Ocarina is a game you can show kids who weren't alive in 1998 and they will feel at home more quickly.

Sometimes the graphical update is really wonderful. The route to Zora's Domain, which I barely remember in the original Ocarina, is now a lovely scramble over cliffs and arcing crags. A bold smattering of 1990s Nickelodeon colours and glossy textures, meanwhile, makes Jabu Jabu's Belly a cross between a pre-millennium rave and a modern soft play.

My favourite locations of all, however, are two of the mid-game dungeons. The Water Temple is now a drowned Art Nouveau palace that you could easily imagine Captain Nemo knocking around in. And the Forest Temple, which is my absolute favourite Zelda dungeon of all time, is a parquet-floored murder mansion that's been overtaken by trees. Dark wood-panelled corridors and weird bits of church sticking out of the foliage. It's the kind of place you'd hear a weird crime podcast about.

Trade-offs, however. My wife, a huge fan of the original game, would wander in and out as I played, and often felt the game she remembered was a little more characterful in its visuals. The moment you fight Dark Link, for example, has lost a little of its glitchy liminality, although the staging, with an old tree in the middle of a vast smoky room, is still wonderfully strange. Towards the end of the game, with the trip into Gerudo territory, you could also occasionally be forgiven for wondering if you'd stepped into one of a dozen third-person Unreal games in development at the moment. It's pleasant to look at, but it sometimes doesn't look specifically like Zelda anymore.

All that, and some strange character models that inevitably I learned to love, don't really matter very much, however. Not least because a handful of clever tweaks elsewhere mean that Ocarina now races along at an astonishing clip. And all this with a careful paring back of intrusions from Navi the fairy and the owl, who were both there in the original game to help move you along swiftly in the first place.

These tweaks are all pretty great. Link now has a jump button, which removes the original game's contextual jumps from the equation, and makes the thundering jump attack even more pleasing to pull off. Even better, in a loan from the 3DS remake of Ocarina, you can swap out usable items using a trigger mini-menu, and you can change boots and whatever you had on your head with some of the directional face buttons.

This doesn't sound like much, but it's quietly transformative in the way that the best updates are. Take the Water Temple. This is the stuff of memes in terms of difficulty and the patience required in navigating an environment that can be flooded up to three different levels. But now, as on the 3DS, you can enjoy it without having to slip into the menu every few steps to add your iron boots or remove them.

And this in turn means that a dungeon I had been really dreading turned out to be a dungeon that revealed itself via experimentation. I would change the water level and see what options I now had, think about the relationship between spaces I could reach and spaces I could not, all without needing to muddle about in menus and interrupt the flow of things. Flow is the word in fact: a simple UI and item-management tweak has given a legendary Zelda dungeon its perfect pace and sense of revelation.

Alongside tweaks like that which I noticed - oh, it's easier to equip the Hookshot - are no doubt hundreds of little things I didn't notice. I suspect there's a lot more gentle direction prompting built into places like the Water Temple, while elsewhere, in the Forest Temple, for example, I suspected that some of the backtracking had been removed. Individual item placements have been changed around perhaps, and there are generous tweaks like a wallet that holds more rupees from the off. For me at least, all of these tweaks had several things in common: they improved the game without removing or altering anything that was particularly meaningful about the original, and, also, I struggled to confidently spot them.

I did try to spot them for a while. And I measured up what I was playing against my memory, which is always wonky in the first place. Hyrule Field feels smaller now, but it's still thrilling to race across. I remember Epona entering the game sooner, or maybe I just remember the idea of a horse in a Zelda game being a huge, attention-holding deal. I thought a favourite boss involving oil paintings came much later, but again, I had just shifted it to the third act because of its original impact on me.

But this gives way over time to the most important thing about Ocarina of Time, I think, and the reason why this remake has such an emotional impact on people like me. This isn't just another Zelda with an ingenious overworld. It's a Zelda game that's even more preoccupied with time than ever before. And this is because time unfolds within the game, via a central mechanic that takes Hyrule seven years into the future, transforming Link from a child to an adult - and then allows you to go back again.

To play a game like this, a game that is about this stuff, after a period of almost thirty years away, gives your imagination and memory a kind of IMAX treatment. I realised that not only is this a game about the passage of time and the way that the world looks different when you're young to when you're a bit older - I had never really realised that adult Link goes through variations of the same dungeons that young Link went through, but now they're all just a bit harder and more consequential - it's also the kind of game that a lot of players have knowingly or unknowingly measured parts of their lives by.

This time, when I reached the first Fairy Fountain, for example, I remembered that my wife had walked down the aisle to this music - about half the registry office recognised the tune with a shiver of laughter, incidentally. Then there's the Water Temple, which has become cultural shorthand for a challenge that is really not screwing around. How many awful things had I faced in life by first conjuring the spirit of Link about to enter this place.

There's that first arrival in Hyrule Field, which is both a promise of everything that games were about to become in 1998 and that fleeting moment in childhood where the boundaries suddenly change. This game doesn't just send me back into my memories, then. It puts me back in conversation with all the people I have known who have ever loved it. I play it now and think I'm talking to my friend who played it at university, or my wife who loved it long before we met.

Was it always this good? Were the dungeons always so complex and challenging, but also so playful, so coherent? Were the bosses always driven by interesting ideas and drama and humour rather than difficulty? Was the world always so rich with minor characters who linger in the mind - the accordion player in the windmill, the gravedigger who has his own tour he'd really like you to try out? It's impossible for me to say at this point. This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday. If you're new to Zelda and you're coming to this game fresh, you're going to love it. Someone, somewhere, is about to play a game so special for the first time that they need to call up their friend and tell them all about it. But if you're returning to this game? Well, somehow you'll find that you're still coming to it fresh.

My dad always said that you should read Don Quixote three times in your life, and I only recently realised that he meant that the book changes because you change. So. When I got to the Deku Tree back at the start of Ocarina a few weeks ago, and I completed the dungeon and watched the impossible vision of the Deku Tree dying of weariness? I remembered that the first time I'd been here, almost thirty years ago, I couldn't help but identify with Link, freshly gifted a sword and shield, one dungeon down, ready for whatever came next. This time, I think, I was closer to identifying with the Deku Tree.

And here's the important part: this wasn't a depressing thought. It just meant that I had taken the long route to reach this point, and this astonishing game had taken the long route too. And yet we arrived at this point together, and together we were transformed. And that's really why any of this video game stuff matters.
