articles.headline: Bonta says he'll counter DOJ election monitors with observers of his own
keyFacts: California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced that his office will deploy state election observers to counter concerns that Justice Department monitors could intimidate voters.
The Justice Department deployed a record 1,000 monitors to all 50 states to ensure election integrity, protect voting rights, and ensure accessibility for voters with disabilities.
Critics including Bonta argued that the large federal presence could discourage voting, while Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon stated monitors would only observe and respect state laws.
body: California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Tuesday afternoon that his office will deploy election observers in response to concerns that Justice Department monitors could intimidate voters.
Bonta said California was taking the same approach it used during the previous two elections, when the state dispatched its own observers alongside federal monitors.

The DOJ's Civil Rights Division has sent 1,000 monitors across the country to ensure election integrity and protect Americans' right to vote , a plan that has been public knowledge for months. The monitors will be personnel from across the DOJ, U.S. Attorney's Offices and employees from the Office of Personnel Management.
The department confirmed Tuesday that while federal election monitoring is routine, this year's operation is the largest in its history, with monitors deployed to all 50 states for the first time.
DOJ FIRES BACK AT DEM AG OVER ELECTION DAY GUIDANCE TELLING OFFICIALS WHEN TO CALL COPS ON FEDERAL AGENTS
The DOJ also released a list of cities where monitors are being deployed. In California, they are being sent to Los Angeles, Alameda, Sacramento and San Diego.
Bonta and other critics have argued that the unusually large federal presence could spook voters or discourage some from casting ballots.

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who leads the Civil Rights Division, told Bloomberg in an August interview that the role of DOJ election monitors would be to observe election practices and pursue investigations into any possible instances of fraud after the fact — not to intervene directly while people are voting.
In Tuesday's announcement, the DOJ added that monitors will also be responsible for ensuring that polling places are accessible for those with disabilities.
DOJ OFFICIAL DEFENDS TRUMP'S NONCITIZEN VOTER PROBE ON '60 MINUTES,' ACCUSES SHOW OF EDITING OUT HER ANSWERS

In her Bloomberg interview, Dhillon said the election monitors would respect the laws of whichever states they end up in. Many states restrict monitors from entering polling places and require them to remain behind designated boundaries outside.
"We respect state law," Dhillon told Bloomberg at the time. "We reach out to the states. If their perimeter is 150 yards, we respect that."

Dhillon also pointed out that the DOJ sent more than 80 monitors to observe primary elections across seven states this year, including locations in Minnesota, Michigan, Florida, Wyoming, South Carolina, Massachusetts and New Hampshire.
The nationwide deployment appeared to be proceeding without major incident Tuesday afternoon, with no significant confrontations involving federal monitors publicly reported.

This comes after the Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration's effort to require California election officials to segregate ballots cast by 20,000 voters the DOJ believes are noncitizens.

articles.headline: Liverpool owner FSG holds talks over buying majority stake in Cadillac F1 team
keyFacts: Fenway Sports Group has held talks about buying a majority stake in the Cadillac Formula One team for over two billion pounds.
Mark Walter is selling sporting assets while under investigation by US authorities for alleged fraud, though TWG has denied any wrongdoing.
FSG is exploring new sporting investments following its recent partial sale of Liverpool FC and its previous experience in NASCAR.
body: Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, has held talks about buying a majority stake in the Cadillac Formula One team for more than £2bn as Mark Walter continues to sell off his sporting assets amid allegations of insurance fraud.

Cadillac entered F1 this year as a joint venture between General Motors and Walter’s TWG Global, which sold its controlling interest in the NBA’s Los Angeles Lakers and a 13% stake in Chelsea this summer, and is also looking to sell Los Angeles Sparks, the WNBA team.

Walter is under investigation by the US Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission over alleged fraud involving the management of funds at his insurance companies Delaware Life, Clear Spring, and EquiTrust. TWG has said “there has been no fraud”.
The 66-year-old Walter is also the controlling owner of Major League Baseball’s Los Angeles Dodgers and insists they will not be sold.

TWG has denied that a sale of Cadillac is imminent, but the Guardian has learned it has had talks with a number of interested parties including FSG, whose sporting investments also include majority stakes in the Boston Red Sox and the NHL team Pittsburgh Penguins.

A source with knowledge of FSG’s plans disclosed that it is looking at other sporting investments after selling 38% of Liverpool this summer to a consortium that includes the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, whose group has also secured the option to complete a full takeover at Anfield before August 2027.

A move by FSG to buy into Cadillac could have implications for its position at Liverpool, which is valued at £5.5bn after this summer’s partial sale, presenting it with the opportunity to make a huge profit after it paid £300m for the entire club in 2010.

FSG has a history of investing in motor sport through its 50% stake in the Nascar team RFK Racing, with the source adding that it has been attracted to F1 by the sport’s remarkable growth over the last decade, particularly in the US.
F1’s annual revenue has more than doubled to $4bn (£3bn) since it was bought by Liberty Media in 2017, and the value of its TV rights continues to increase.
Sportico has previously reported that Walter values his Cadillac shareholding at about £2.24bn. The size of TWG’s and General Motors’ respective stakes has never been made public.
Cadillac are bottom of the constructors’ championship in their debut season and have yet to win a point.
FSG declined to comment on its investment plans.

articles.headline: Why did voters (finally) hand Trump a historic defeat?
keyFacts: Democrats won a historic national victory in the 2026 elections, gaining at least 255 House seats and leading major Senate battlegrounds.
Rising energy costs from tariffs and war in Iran, alongside aggressive ICE enforcement, contributed to massive Republican losses among voters.
The article notes that future Republican leaders may hesitate before starting new trade wars or aggressive federal enforcement actions.
body: Texas Democratic Senate candidate State Rep. James Talarico greets supporters outside Whataburger on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. Talarico won big Tuesday night. | Sergio Flores/Getty Images

On May 3, 2016 — the night Donald Trump effectively clinched the Republican Party’s presidential nomination for the first time — then-Sen. Lindsey Graham tweeted , “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed…….and we will deserve it.”

Graham was scarcely alone in voicing such sentiments. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, former Gov. Jeb Bush , and most political analysts said much the same thing. After all, how could nominating an unpopular, profane, and authoritarian reality star — with more expertise in stiffing contractors than formulating policies — lead a major political party to anything but ruin?
On Tuesday night, the reckoning that Graham had prophesied finally arrived, just a decade behind schedule.

As of this writing, the Democratic Party appears all but certain to win nine of the cycle’s top 10 Senate battleground states, including perennial bastions of Republicanism like Kansas, Texas, and South Carolina. And Democrats are favored to prevail in the 10th battleground (Alaska), while winning at least 255 House seats. Then there’s an 11th race almost no one saw coming (Mississippi) that is heading down to the wire. The party’s share of the national congressional vote isn’t entirely clear. But many analysts expect it to be the largest that either party has won since the 1970s.
Among the many Republicans felled by this “blue tsunami” was Graham’s own sister, Darline, whom Trump handpicked as the GOP’s nominee in South Carolina, after Lindsey died earlier this year.

From one angle, these results are astonishing. We have not seen a wave this large in half a century. And every previous post-2016 election cast doubt on whether such a Democratic rout was even possible. After all, Democrats won a national landslide in the 2018 midterms, but nevertheless failed to gain Senate control, as red-state electorates still proved largely unwilling to back Democratic candidates.

Conventional wisdom held that the nationalization of elections — and polarization of voters — had brought an end to the era when idiosyncratic Democratic candidates could compete in overwhelmingly Republican states.
No longer. Tuesday’s results look like precisely what many expected in early 2016, before Trump proved himself more politically formidable than most of his critics had imagined.
All of which raises the question: Why now? Why did Trump manage to provoke an epochal rebuke from American voters in 2026, but not in preceding elections?
It’s partly “the economy, stupid”
The most plausible answer is, to quote the legendary Democratic consultant James Carville, “the economy, stupid.”

As 2016 made clear, the American electorate didn’t consider Trump’s illiberalism or inexperience as disqualifying as mainstream elites did. And some believed that the business executive would be well-suited to manage the economy, or at least, bring about a measure of welcome economic change.

For much of his first term, Trump appeared to validate this impression, presiding over low inflation and full employment. In December 2019, a CNN poll found voters more satisfied with the US economy than they’d been in nearly two decades. (Of course, 2020 would bring economic upheaval, but many Americans didn’t consider Trump culpable for the pandemic.)
Trump’s apparent economic efficacy put a floor beneath his approval and the GOP’s electoral performances during term one. And it made him a somewhat more credible anti-inflation candidate in 2024.

Upon reelection, however, Trump showed less than zero interest in containing the cost of living. Rather, he actively pushed up prices by imposing large tariffs on most imported goods and triggering a global energy crisis with his war in Iran.
The latter proved particularly consequential. Between February (when the war began) and Election Day, Americans’ energy costs skyrocketed along with the Democrats’ polling advantage.
The whole “authoritarian nightmare” thing also mattered

Although the economic context is likely the biggest single driver of the GOP’s belated reckoning, it is not sufficient to explain it. The 2026 economy isn’t great. But it also isn’t a total disaster. America’s inflation rate is a bit under 4 percent; in November 2022, when Joe Biden suffered a much smaller midterm rebuke, it was over 7 percent. Our nation’s unemployment rate, meanwhile, sits at 4.2 percent; in November 2010, it was nearly 10 percent, yet the GOP won a smaller share of the national vote than Democrats apparently did Tuesday night.
To explain the scale of the GOP’s drubbing then, we can’t rely on material factors alone.

It is true that Trump has been an illiberal demagogue from the moment he launched his candidacy in 2015 . And of course, he incited an insurrectionary riot on Capitol Hill in 2021 without squandering his political viability.

Nevertheless, the cruel and authoritarian character of Trump’s political project was more naked over the past two years than ever before. The first Trump administration did not tweet out white nationalist slogans from federal agency accounts on a regular basis. More critically, it did not ramp up interior immigration enforcement to the degree that the second Trump White House has.

The indiscriminate nature of ICE enforcement over the past two years alienated many Latino voters , who had warmed to Trump in 2024. A recent NBC News/Telemundo poll found that 65 percent of Latino voters disapproved of ICE, while nearly a quarter said they personally knew someone who was detained or deported over the past two years. On Tuesday night, Latino counties swung massively against Republicans.

Meanwhile, Trump’s willingness to condone ICE agents ’ killing of two US citizens — combined with his broader assaults on civil liberties and government integrity — may have energized his opposition to an unprecedented extent.
The costs of Trumpism could linger

It is still unclear whether the GOP will pay a lasting price for its Faustian bargain with Trump. In early 2016 — before he himself became a Trump toady — Lindsey Graham predicted that a Trump nomination would not only cost the Republicans the 2016 election but “destroy the party for decades to come.”

There is little chance that the GOP will be politically irrelevant for a generation. But precisely how it will wriggle out of the corner that Trump has led it into remains to be seen. The party plainly needs to distinguish its brand from the president’s. Yet its remaining elected officials are overwhelmingly from deeply pro-Trump jurisdictions. And unlike George W. Bush after 2008 , Trump is unlikely to quietly abide his party disowning him.

Whatever the future brings, Republicans will not soon forget a loss of this magnitude. Tuesday’s results are unlikely to cure the GOP of its taste for illiberal demagogy. But the next GOP leader may hesitate before launching new trade (or actual) wars, winking at neo-Nazis, or letting federal agents execute American citizens.
The political costs of Trumpism were, in fact, exceptionally high. It just took 10 years for the bill to come due.

articles.headline: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?
keyFacts: Companies are creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles to manage AI tools, automate tasks, and develop internal agents, according to the article.
PwC research found that entry-level roles influenced by AI are seven times more likely to require senior-level skills like strategic decision making.
Some industry figures, such as Simon Pratt and Claire Reid, caution that graduates must still learn traditional sector knowledge alongside AI skills for long-term career progression.
body: - Published
Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.
Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.

She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.
A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.
Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others.
"A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.
AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts, but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.

Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.

Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI.
"My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.
Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.
CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI.

"We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell.
"We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."

Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."

If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.
Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.

For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, external, it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.
Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.

Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks.

"Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23.
"I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to."
His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result.
"AI is killing the 'pyramid' approachâ¦progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton.
'Learning the trade'
There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.
But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?
Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team.
"There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.

Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade".
"Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains.

"They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."
Claire Reid, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression.
"There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reid.
"But AI skills on their own are not going to help you in your career. You've got to couple that with that sector knowledge of what that client actually wants."
Back in Coventry, Dillan Patel is confident his AI work will continue to be valuable, and he wants to keep building on it.

"I don't think I'd want to explore different positions within the business. Through my involvement in AI-related projects, I already work closely with different areas of the business and I'm gaining valuable knowledge and experience along the way," he says.

articles.headline: California fights "preposterous" Trump admin demand to scrap state broadband laws
keyFacts: California accepted $1.42 billion in federal broadband funds while rejecting the Trump administration's demand to scrap its net neutrality and telecom laws.
State officials argued in a letter to the NTIA that the federal demand violates California's constitutional rights and exceeds legal authority.
The dispute could lead to legal battles and may cause California to delay or cancel its distribution of the federal broadband grants.
body: California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration’s demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations.

California’s stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds.

The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction.

State officials argue that California should be able to obtain the money and keep enforcing its laws because the Trump administration’s demand would violate the state’s constitutional rights. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) made its view clear in a carefully worded letter yesterday to Assistant Secretary of Commerce and NTIA Administrator Arielle Roth.

“The CPUC cannot be bound by any terms or conditions that are unconstitutional or not authorized by law and it expressly does not waive or concede any arguments or challenges concerning the legality, interpretation, or applicability of any term or condition,” CPUC President John Reynolds told Roth.

Reynolds’ letter also said the CPUC cannot prevent other California agencies from enforcing state laws, suggesting that the attorney general would maintain the right to punish misbehaving Internet providers.

articles.headline: Japan faces diplomatic dilemma amid joint pressure from nuclear neighbors
keyFacts: Russian security agents detained Japanese journalist Yuki Imai on espionage charges, which the Japanese government denies.
Japan faces mounting diplomatic pressure and tensions from neighboring nuclear powers Russia and China amid a long-standing territorial dispute.
Experts stated that Japan is concerned it may not receive sufficient support from the United States amidst these escalating regional tensions.
body: Japan faces diplomatic dilemma amid joint pressure from nuclear neighbors
As the Ukraine war grinds on, ties between Russia and neighboring Japan are at their worst in decades. Tokyo wants more support from Washington, but some Japanese are concerned they may not get it.
AILSA CHANG, HOST:

And now to Russia's war in Ukraine. This war has raised tensions not only in Europe but also in Asia. Ties between Russia and neighboring Japan are at their worst in decades. Tokyo would like more support from Washington, but as NPR's Anthony Kuhn reports, some Japanese people are concerned they may not get it.
ANTHONY KUHN, BYLINE: In a video released by Russia's federal security bureau, FSB agents charge into a hotel room on Sakhalin Island in Russia's Far East on October 13.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED FSB AGENT: (Non-English language spoken).
YUKI IMAI: (Non-English language spoken).

KUHN: The agents pin Japanese journalist Yuki Imai to the ground and handcuff him. They question him and take him to Moscow to face trial on charges of espionage. Japan's government denies the charges. The FSB says Imai was reporting on soldiers from Russia's Far East who were deployed to Ukraine. Shinji Hyodo, a Russia expert at the National Institute for Defense Studies in Tokyo, argues that the journalist was just doing his job.
SHINJI HYODO: (Through interpreter) I believe the Russian side intends to use this as a political bargaining chip to exert pressure on Japan.
KUHN: Hyodo says that underlying the current tensions are Japan's sanctions on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine. Russia now sees Japan as hostile, and bilateral relations have gone into a tailspin.

HYODO: (Through interpreter) I think it's fair to say that Japan is currently facing its greatest diplomatic challenge since the end of the war. This is no longer just a bilateral issue between Japan and Russia.

KUHN: There's also what Hyodo calls the China factor. China has been putting pressure on Japan since last year, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said that a Chinese blockade of Taiwan could justify a Japanese military response. Russia relies on China's support in its war on Ukraine, and it's joined China in pressuring Japan. Another factor is a long-running territorial dispute between Russia and Japan.
(SOUNDBITE OF FACTORY MACHINERY)

KUHN: In August, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited a seafood factory, hospital and school on his first visit to one of four disputed islands called the Southern Kurils by Russia and the Northern Territories by Japan. The Soviet Union seized the islands at the end of World War II. They never signed a permanent peace treaty because of the dispute and because the U.S. warned them not to. This episode was called the Dulles intervention. James Brown, an expert on Japan-Russia relations at Temple University in Tokyo, explains.

JAMES BROWN: This was the suggestion from John Foster Dulles, the secretary of state, in 1956 that if Japan were to make an agreement with the Soviet Union, settling the territorial dispute, well, then perhaps the United States would remain forevermore in holding, administering Okinawa.

KUHN: So the Soviet Union kept the islands, and the U.S. returned to Japan the island of Okinawa, which remains a key U.S. military hub in Asia. Brown says Japan's media generally don't mention the U.S.'s role in the territorial dispute so as not to offend its only ally as it faces three nuclear powers - Russia, China and North Korea.

BROWN: Japan's situation is essentially they have no Plan B, which means that they have to rely on the United States. They have to flatter the Trump administration. They have to do everything possible to avoid abandonment.

KUHN: The U.S. has criticized Russia's arrest of the Japanese journalist, but Shinji Hyodo says that the U.S. generally doesn't seem very interested in Japan's conflict with Russia. And he says Japan is concerned about the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, this month.

HYODO: (Through interpreter) There is a possibility that a trilateral summit involving the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia could take place, potentially leading to the U.S. being swayed toward the positions held by China and Russia.
KUHN: It's unclear whether Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will meet with either Russian or Chinese leaders at the summit. Anthony Kuhn, NPR News, Seoul.
